activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral law, was compiled around 200 CE under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi.
story:
Grandmother's dining room table still smelled of lemon polish, and Maelie spread her index cards across it with the feeling of conducting a small, private war. The debate was in four days. The resolution, which Mr. Novák had written on the board in his narrow hand, was that the ancient prohibition on work during the Sabbath no longer made sense in modern life, and the rule of the assignment was cruel and simple: you could only argue from the text itself. No philosophers, no opinions, no Wikipedia. She had agreed to take the affirmative side because Cohen had asked her to, or because she had volunteered before he could, depending on which version of that afternoon you believed. Anika insisted it was the second. Anika insisted a lot of things.

"The problem," Maelie said aloud to the empty room, "is that the Torah never defines work." She had read the passages three times. Six days you shall labor, and on the seventh you shall rest, and whoever does work on it shall be cut off. It was like being told to avoid a thing that no one would name. She had built her whole case on that absence, on the argument that a rule without a definition was a rule that had already stopped applying, and she had been rather proud of it, the way you are proud of a bridge before anyone drives a truck over it.

Her grandmother was out at her garden club, so Maelie went to the shelves in the study, the shelf of leather spines her grandfather had left behind, the ones nobody touched. She was looking for a commentary, anything, and she was not snooping, whatever Anika would say. Near the bottom, wedged sideways, she found a small blue volume with gold lettering. She opened it and the pages mesmerized her, not with beauty but with density, argument stacked on argument, rabbis disagreeing in neat, numbered rows.

She carried it to the kitchen table and read while the kettle ticked. It took her a while to understand what she was holding. When Mr. Novák came by at five to return the hedge clippers, she met him at the gate with the book held open like evidence.

"Is this what I think it is?" she asked.

"The Mishnah," he said. "First major written collection of the oral law. Your grandfather studied it." He looked at the page she had marked, and then at her, and said nothing more, which was his way of making you do the work.

She sat on the back steps and read until the light went amber. Somewhere in the tractate called Shabbat, in a discussion she had to read four times, the rabbis catalogued the categories of forbidden labor, the whole architecture of what counted as work, and she found a note in her grandfather's handwriting in the margin giving a date. The book had been compiled around the year 200, under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi. The Torah did not list what counted as work because the listing had happened later, in this book, in these rows of argument. Her bridge collapsed in a warm, quiet rush. She had built her affirmative case on an absence that was not an absence at all, only a gap between two texts, and someone had filled it eighteen hundred years ago.

Anika came over after dinner, and they sat on the porch with the index cards between them.

"My whole case is specious," Maelie said. "I argued from silence and the silence turned out to be a different book."

"Then argue that," Anika said, eating a plum. "The rule isn't just the verse. It's the whole chain of people deciding what it means. If the definition was made by people, people can unmake it."

"But that cuts both ways. If they could define it, they could redefine it, which means the rule isn't dead, it's alive and adjustable, which is the opposite of what I'm supposed to prove." Maelie turned a card over and wrote nothing on it. She was thinking about her grandfather's margin note, about the ontology of a rule, whether a law was the words on the scroll or the mountain of argument underneath, and she understood that she did not know, and that not knowing was suddenly the most interesting thing she had.

Cohen texted at nine to ask if she was ready to crush him. She typed "absolutely" and deleted it, typed it again, and set the phone face down on the rail. In the morning she would rebuild the case from the blue volume, or she would concede it, or she would stand up in Mr. Novák's classroom and say that the honest answer was somewhere she hadn't reached yet.

She carried the book inside, and her grandmother, home at last, saw it in her hands and paused in the doorway with her hat still on.

"You found his shelf," her grandmother said.

Maelie held it out to her, open to the page with the note in the margin.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
Cohen had written the heading before he thought about it, the way his hand knew how to write his own name. Works Cited, centered at the bottom of page eleven, under a research paper about the Bracero program that had taken him three weekends and one fight with his father about the kitchen table. Mr. Ivanova had asked for a bibliography. Cohen knew this. He had read the assignment sheet twice. But two years of Ms. Audrey's English class had trained something deeper than memory, and now he sat at home on Thursday night staring at the heading, wondering whether he had just failed.

In the fall, English had been simple in a way he missed. "MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading Works Cited," Audrey had told him back then, voluble as always, leaning across the library table to tap his draft. She was the one person in that class who actually read the style guide for fun. Cohen had metabolized the rule without effort because she made it sound like gossip, like something worth knowing, and every paper since had carried the small clean parentheses like signatures. (Vasquez 44). (Vasquez 61). He had been proud of them.

Mr. Ivanova was not proud of anything on Thursday nights. He was a man who returned drafts with a single note at the top, and Cohen's note, on the first history paper of the semester, had read: "This is an argument, not a report. Good. Footnotes, not parentheses. Bibliography, not Works Cited. See me." Cohen had not seen him. He had gone home, opened the school database, and tried to figure out footnotes alone, which was like trying to learn a language by reading its dictionary.

On Friday afternoon he emailed him instead, because saying things out loud to Mr. Ivanova felt like standing in front of a machine with unknown throughput, never sure how much of you would be processed and what would come out the other side. "I don't understand why history needs a bibliography when English uses Works Cited," he wrote. "Is it just a different word for the same thing, or are the rules actually different? I don't want to guess again." He read the email four times before sending it, deleted one apology, and kept the question.

The reply came at 9:40 that night, while Cohen sat at the kitchen table pushing rice around his plate. "Different fields, different conventions," Mr. Ivanova wrote. "Historians want to see where every claim comes from, in detail, at the bottom of the page. Your English training isn't wrong. It's just not ours. Come Monday with a question about your argument, not your formatting. The formatting you can fix. The argument is what I grade." Cohen read it twice, then a third time, and noticed something he hadn't expected: the email was kind. Not warm, exactly. Kind in the way of a person who had decided years ago that honesty was a form of respect.

Saturday, Billie came over with two energy drinks and her own history draft, which she claimed was "a disaster in progress." They spread both papers across the kitchen table and tried to convert his parenthetical citations into footnotes by hand. "Okay, so this one, Vasquez 44," she said, tapping his page. "In your English class that just goes in the parentheses at the end of the sentence. But here you need the little number, and then the whole thing about the book down at the bottom." Cohen typed the number, then the note below, and saw how the page looked different immediately, how the evidence sat underneath the argument like a foundation you could actually walk around and inspect. "It's slower," he said. "It's way slower." "It's not slower," Billie said. "It's just honest in a different direction."

He kept the Works Cited page anyway, printed it separately, and stapled it behind the bibliography like an appendix of his own thinking. He wasn't sure that was allowed. He wasn't sure he cared. Somewhere between Audrey's parentheses and Mr. Ivanova's footnotes there was a position he could actually hold, which was that both systems were attempts at the same honesty, and that he wanted to be fluent in both without pretending either one was the truth. What stayed uncertain was whether Mr. Ivanova would see the extra page as effort or as defiance, and Cohen could not make that not matter to him.

Monday morning he walked into third period and set the paper on the desk before the bell. Mr. Ivanova flipped to the last page, then past it, and held up the Works Cited sheet between two fingers.

"Your idea, or your mistake?"

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
Thomas had the score open on the kitchen table and the headphones half off one ear, because the toaster had started to smell like burning again and he didn't trust it. The assignment was due Monday: analyse the first movement of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A minor, mark the exposition, the development, the recapitulation, and hand in something Mr. Krause would not immediately return with a single question mark pencilled in the margin. He had three coloured pens and a printout that already looked like a bird had fought over it.

Mariana came through the back door without knocking, holding her phone in one hand and a bag of apricots in the other. She had a theory that Thomas's mother kept the only house on the street where the kettle worked properly. She put the phone down on the table, plugged it into the little speaker he kept next to the fruit bowl, and started the recording she'd found, a live performance from some festival she'd never heard of.

"I'm using this for my essay too," she said. "This pianist. Listen to how she takes the second theme."

They listened. Thomas followed the bars with his finger, colouring the exposition in blue, and had just drawn his arrow toward the development, where he expected the music to move into minor keys and start breaking apart, when the pianist went back to the beginning. The opening theme started over, exactly as before. Mariana stopped the track.

"She messed up," Mariana said. "She lost her place and went back."

"In a live performance? At a festival?" Thomas turned the score around to face her and tapped the page. "Look. There are repeat signs here, at the start and the end of this whole section. The double bars with the dots."

"So it's written in?"

"In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs," Thomas said, and then heard how it sounded, like he was reading from a textbook, and added, "so the performer plays it twice before the development begins." He had written a note in the margin two days ago and only understood it now, holding his finger against the page while the music restarted in his headphones from where Mariana had paused it.

Mariana ate an apricot and thought about it. Her essay was due Monday too, and she had built half of it around the idea that the pianist shaped the opening with a kind of hesitancy that paid off later. "But then the second time through, she plays it differently," she said. "Listen. The left hand comes in louder. She's not repeating it, she's revising it."

They played it again, both times through, and she was right about the left hand. Thomas marked it in the score. This was the problem he kept running into: Mr. Krause wanted the form, the clean architecture, first theme, transition, second theme, closing section, and Thomas could see it, he could draw the boxes. But the recording kept refusing to be a diagram. The repeat, which he had first dismissed as some eighteenth-century contrivance, a piece of machinery nobody needed anymore, turned out to be where the performance actually lived. The pianist played the exposition once as a question and once as something closer to an answer, and Thomas had no box for that.

His father came in, looked at the toaster, which was now smoking faintly, unplugged it, and left again without comment, the way he dealt with most things in the kitchen.

"Maybe that's the essay," Mariana said. She had pulled her notebook toward her and was writing fast, which she did when she'd found an angle, and she never shared the angle until she'd finished the sentence. "The form is the frame, and the repeat is where the performer gets to argue with it."

"Krause will say I'm avoiding the analysis."

"Then give him the analysis and then tell him what happens the second time." She slid her notes across. "You can have that part. I'm writing about the closing theme, which nobody ever writes about, which is why I'm writing about it."

Thomas looked at his blue pen, then at the second pass of the exposition, which he had begun marking in red because it felt like a different event. Two hearings of the same bars, one obedient and one restless, and the development only beginning after both. He thought about writing that the repeat existed to teach the listener the material, then thought that was exactly the kind of explanation Krause crossed out, some neat little machine of a reason. He didn't know why the repeat was there. He knew only that it was there, and that the pianist used it, and that his page now had two colours where the form said there should be one.

He drew a vertical line down the margin and wrote on the left side, exposition, first time, and on the right side, exposition, second time, and between them a question mark he decided he would leave in even if it cost him the mark.

"Play it once more," he said. "From the repeat sign."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
The cultural center smelled of fried potatoes and wet wool, and Maria told Christopher, again, that she had this under control. She had said it in the car, and again at the coat rack, and now a third time as Ms. Nakamura from the community board handed her the box of candles, because saying it made it closer to true. Fourth night, the schedule said. Maria, 7:15, menorah lighting. She had volunteered in a moment of something she did not want to examine, and since then she had been telling people it was for her grandmother, who loved Hanukkah, who taught her the blessings when she was six and made her enunciate every word until the Hebrew came out clean as glass.

The menorah sat on a folding table near the windows, old brass gone dull at the joints, and Maria lifted it and felt its surprising weight, like a small animal settling. That was when the trouble started. She counted the branches. Eight, she thought, and counted again, and got nine, and counted a third time with her finger hovering above the metal so Christopher could not accuse her of skipping one. Nine branches. She stood there while the room filled behind her, kids darting between folding chairs, someone's toddler escalating toward a tantrum, and felt the interminable minute stretch out, the kind that makes you aware of your own hands.

"You're staring at it," Christopher said. He had followed her over, holding a paper plate of latkes he was not eating.

"I'm counting it," she said. "There are nine."

"So?"

"So there are eight nights. I learned that before I learned to read. Eight nights, eight candles." She turned the menorah, checking whether one branch hid behind another, some trick of the weld. It did not. Nine arms, evenly spaced, and no error she could find in the object itself, which left the error somewhere less comfortable.

Jordan appeared at her shoulder, the way Jordan did, already halfway into someone else's problem. "You put in the wrong amount?"

"There is no wrong amount. There are nine holes and eight nights, apparently, which is like the holiday secretly failing math." She was aware she sounded certain, a tone she had inherited and did not always deserve. Last year she had told her grandmother she was too busy with finals to come to this exact room, this exact event, and her grandmother had said that was fine, and it had not been fine, and Maria had spent a year being the kind of person who said the word fine.

Jordan leaned in, squinting. "Maybe one's a spare?"

"Menorahs don't have spares." But she picked up a candle and turned it in her fingers, and thought about the way her grandmother always lit one candle first, from the match, before anything else happened, and used it on the others. A memory surfaced that Maria had filed under unimportant: the way her grandmother held that first candle higher, apart, like it was staff rather than cast. She had never asked why. There had been an interminable number of things she had never asked why, a whole attic of them, and now the door to the attic was locked.

The room was quieting. Ms. Nakamura was moving toward the microphone, which meant Maria had about ninety seconds. She set the candles in the holders, right to left, four of them, because four nights had passed, and then she held the ninth candle and looked at it and thought, helper. Her grandmother must have said it. The ninth is the shamash, the helper. It must have been said over her head a hundred times, in that dry voice, while Maria doodled on the synagogue bulletin, and she had let it pour through her like water through a net.

She struck the match. "Fourth night," she announced to the room, to the kids cross-legged on the floor, to Christopher and Jordan and a woman holding her phone up sideways, and her voice did not shake, which she noted with a small distant pride. She lit the shamash first and then, from it, each of the four in turn, and her grandmother's blessings came out of her mouth more or less whole, one or two syllables slipping, the rest clean. She had expected to feel worse, telling everyone this was for her grandmother, standing there alone at the table where her grandmother used to stand, having spent a year telling people she was at these things with her family when her family had stopped coming altogether after the funeral. She had even told Christopher that her mother was in the back room helping with the food. There was no mother in the back room. There was a table of donated pastries and a teenager refilling juice.

Afterward, Christopher found her by the window. "Nice job," he said. "You looked like you'd done it a thousand times."

"I have," she said, which was true in the ways that mattered and false in the ones that didn't, and she watched the four small flames lean as someone opened the far door, all of them bending together, then standing back up.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
The letterbox was half a metre from the front door, but Simon made the walk last longer by circling the lamppost first, the way he had every afternoon for eleven days. Nothing today either, only a takeaway menu and a gas bill addressed to his mother. He stood there with the mail against his chest and admitted, for the first time, that he had no idea which answer he was hoping for.

It had started in September, in Mr. Nolan's chemistry room after the last bell, when the smell of sulphur still hung in the air and Mr. Nolan was packing away the samples with the unhurried care of a man who trusted the next day to arrive. Simon had lingered to ask about personal statements, and Mr. Nolan had said, "You're doing the UK system, aren't you. UCAS. So you can pick up to five courses, and they go down in no order of preference. Universities don't see a ranking. It's just a list." Simon had written it on the back of his hand. Five slots. No favourites declared. It had sounded like freedom at the time.

The freedom turned out to be its own kind of arithmetic. His mother wanted economics at a London university, something that would amortize the cost of all those years of tutoring by leading to a salary with a comma in it. Simon wanted chemistry, or possibly history of science, or possibly marine biology, which he had liked since a documentary at age nine and had not thought about since. He spread the prospectuses across his bed like a dealer laying out cards, and Odin, sprawled on the floor with Simon's laptop, kept scrolling the league tables and saying "this one's ranked higher, this one's ranked higher," as if the rankings would make the decision for him.

Holden took the opposite view, which was Holden's way. "Just pick the five you'd actually go to," he said on the walk home, kicking a bottle cap along the gutter. "If you wouldn't go, the slot's wasted, and you've only got five. They're all the same size." Simon had started to argue and then stopped, because Holden was right about the slots being the same size and wrong, Simon thought, about everything else. The same size was the point. Since the list declared no order, no course was a reach and none was a safety; they sat there flat and equal, and the sorting had to happen inside him instead of on paper. He envied people who could be doctrinaire about themselves, who could say I am this and not that, and close doors without flinching.

He had narrowed it by a kind of chemistry of his own. On a rainy Wednesday he told Odin that choosing felt like allotropes, the way carbon could be graphite or diamond, same element, different arrangement, and Odin had laughed at him for a full minute and then gone quiet and said, "Yeah, actually." Simon filed chemistry at three universities, history of science at one, and, after a long night in which he did not do his maths homework, marine biology at a coastal campus that Odin had never heard of and Holden called "the seal college." His mother read the final list at the kitchen table, turning her teaspoon slowly, and said only, "No economics." The teaspoon went around twice more before she said, "It's your five." Not his five choices, exactly. Just his five, like something he had been given to carry.

Then the waiting, which was nothing like he had imagined. He had thought waiting would be passive, but it turned out to be work. He checked the online portal the way other people bit their nails, and every evening he walked to the mailbox in the blue half-light, past the hedge that smelled of wet leaves, and reached in through the cold metal throat of it for an envelope that was not there yet.

The twelfth day, there was one. Thick, cream-coloured, his name typed in a font that looked older than he was. He did not open it at the mailbox. He carried it back up the path, turning it over, feeling the weight of it, which told him nothing, because everyone knew a thin envelope meant no and a thick one might mean yes, and everyone also knew that meant nothing. At the door he stopped, one hand on the latch, and realized he still could not say which answer he wanted. Two offers, or all five, or none, and whichever came, he would still be the same boy who could not rank himself, standing at a door with a letter he had not opened.

He opened it standing on the step, the porch light coming on above him because it had grown dark without his noticing. He read the first line, and then he read it again.

From the kitchen, his mother's voice: "Well? Is it good news?"

Simon folded the letter back along its crease and said, "It's one of them."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
Jayden had avoided the study for three weeks, which was easy because the funeral was over and everyone had gone back to pretending. But his grandmother had to move out of the house by the end of the month, and on Saturday morning she stood in the doorway with two empty boxes and didn't say anything, just held them out, and that was harder to refuse than crying would have been. So he took the boxes and started with the desk, where his grandfather had kept forty years of papers in an order only he understood.

Genesis came by at noon with a bag of Chinese food from the place on Delancey, because she had heard about the move from Kohen and because she was better at showing up than at saying why. She sat cross-legged on the floor and sorted receipts into piles while Jayden worked through the bottom drawer. He was morose in a way he recognized and didn't like, answering her questions in single syllables, and she let him be that way without denigrating it or trying to fix it, which was the particular thing Genesis was good at.

The photo album was wedged under a shelf of dictionaries. Not the family albums from the living room; a smaller one, green cover cracked at the spine, that Jayden had never seen. Inside were pictures of his grandfather as a young man, skinny, in a windbreaker, standing at a cemetery gate. Then the same cemetery in different springs across decades: his grandfather with a broom, his grandfather wiping a headstone with a rag, his grandfather arranging what looked like dumplings and oranges on the grass in front of a name Jayden couldn't read in the faded photograph. The last photo was dated six years ago. His grandfather was holding the broom and half smiling at whoever took the picture.

"What is this," Jayden said, not really a question.

Genesis leaned over. She turned a page, then another, and her face changed the way it did when she solved something before he did. "Qingming," she said. "My grandma's family does this. Every spring, on April 4th, 5th, or 6th, depending on the year." She tapped the broom in the photo. "You go to your ancestors' graves and sweep them, clean them, and leave food."

Jayden looked at the dumplings in the photograph, at the oranges arranged in a careful line, and something assembled itself in him slowly, the way his grandfather used to do puzzles, edges first. His grandfather had gone every spring, or nearly every spring, for forty years, and had never once taken Jayden, and had never once mentioned it. He felt the sting of that before he felt anything else, the sense of being left out of a room in the house he thought he knew completely.

But then he found the notebook tucked behind the albums, and it was a different story. His grandfather's handwriting, small and slanted: dates going back decades, and beside each date a note. Weather. Who came. One entry from six years ago read, Jayden too young yet, next year maybe, and the next year read, knee bad, went alone. The years after that just said, went alone, went alone, went alone. The last entry, from last April, two months before the hospital, said only, soon tell him.

Genesis read over his shoulder and didn't say anything for a minute. Then she said, "There's still time this year. Qingming's in like two weeks."

His grandmother was in the kitchen wrapping dishes in newspaper. Jayden stood in the doorway holding the green album and the notebook, and he understood that he could be angry about the lost years or he could be grateful for the last two weeks, and that these were not actually opposites, that he could hold both, though which one would win in the long run he couldn't yet say. "Nai Nai," he said, which was not what he'd planned to say, using the name for the first time since the funeral. "Can you show me where his father is buried?"

She set down the dish. She looked at the album, and at him, and wiped her hands on her apron as though what came next required clean hands.

On the sixth of April they took the bus out past the cemetery gate in the photographs. His grandmother carried a broom she had brought from the old house, the actual broom, and Jayden hadn't known she'd thought to pack it. He swept the stone while she wiped it down with a rag, and it was simpler than he expected, the work of it, no gravitas arriving from anywhere, just dust and cold air and his arms getting tired. Then she unpacked the container she'd been carrying and set out dumplings, still warm, and two oranges, and Jayden placed them in a line because that was how the photograph had shown it. He wasn't sure his grandfather could see, or receive, or whatever the right verb was, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he might never be sure. But he took the notebook out of his jacket and read the dates aloud, one by one, all forty years of them, while his grandmother held the broom and listened, and when he reached the last entry he closed the book and said, "He was going to tell me."

"I know," his grandmother said, and reached over and straightened the second orange so it sat square with the first.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
Oliver had taped the inflation graph to the inside of the lemonade stand's plywood counter, where the customers couldn't see it, and every time the pitcher ran low he crouched down and studied the line that climbed and climbed and then, in 1980, fell off a cliff. He was supposed to present this thing to his economics class at two o'clock, and it was already eleven, and all he could say with any confidence was the sentence Mr. Ramos had written on the board: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. Somewhere between the board and his own mouth, the explanation kept disappearing.

"You're scaring the customers," Khadija said. She was on the stool by the cash box, counting quarters into stacks of five. "Every time you duck down there you come up looking like you saw a ghost."

"US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," Oliver said. He said it the way he'd been saying it all morning, flat, like a password he hoped would open something. "And then it fell below 3 percent by 1983. That's the whole mystery. That's what I have to explain."

Arjun arrived on his bike with one hand on the handlebars and the other holding a bag of ice, which he dropped into the cooler before he even said hello. He had promised to be Oliver's practice audience, mostly because Oliver had promised him free lemonade for a week, and he pulled a chair up to the front of the stand and folded his arms in a way that was supposed to look like a teacher's. "Go ahead," he said. "Pretend I'm your class. Pretend I know nothing."

Oliver stood up straight, adjusted an imaginary tie, and began. "Inflation is when prices go up." He stopped. That part he owned. It was the next part, the part about the central bank and the interest rates, that turned to fog whenever he reached for it. He tried again, using a comparison his father had made once at dinner, something about pulling a car over before fixing the engine, and Khadija frowned and said that made it sound like the Fed was punishing everybody for something the money had done, which didn't seem fair.

A woman with a stroller bought two cups, and while Oliver poured, he kept thinking about her, about the quarters she'd counted out of a zippered pouch, about how a person decides whether to spend or to save. Something about her purse stayed with him after she'd gone. He turned to the graph again. The steep drop in the early eighties wasn't magic and it wasn't punishment. Maybe it was more like the whole country deciding, all at once, that borrowing was suddenly expensive and saving was suddenly worth it, everyone pulling back a little, and all those little pullbacks adding up to the line bending downward. He didn't know if that was exactly right, but it felt like something he could stand behind, and he said so, out loud, to the ice chest.

"That's better," Arjun said. "Except you said 'maybe' four times."

"I know." Oliver filled his own cup and drank half of it in one go. "That's the honest part. I can tell them what happened. Inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980, and after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases, it fell below 3 percent by 1983. That's solid. Why the rates did it, I can only get most of the way."

"Then say that," Khadija said. "Mr. Ramos keeps telling you your elocution is fine and your certainty is the problem. Say the fact like it's a fact and the rest like it's your thinking. Nobody's asking you to emancipate the truth from all doubt. You're sixteen."

Oliver laughed, which he hadn't done since breakfast, and it loosened something in his chest. He tried the whole explanation once more, all the way through, hands still damp from the pitcher, and this time he let the uncertain part be uncertain out loud, and neither of them winced. His approach wasn't going to be the cerebral performance he'd planned, all clean chains of logic; it was going to be a person standing in front of a graph, saying what he knew and marking the edge of what he didn't.

At noon Mr. Ramos came by on his walk, as he did most Saturdays, and bought a cup with a dollar and told Oliver to keep the change. He asked, mildly, whether the presentation was ready. Oliver looked at the graph taped to the counter, then at his two friends, then at the quarter Khadija was holding out to him, heads up, as if it were a small coin-sized microphone.

"Ready enough," Oliver said, and took the quarter.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Lynn Hunt's 1984 book Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution.
story:
The archive kept its blinds drawn against the August afternoon, and the fluorescent hush inside seemed to enervate Evan more than the heat ever had. He had been assigned, three weeks ago, an essay on how interpretations of the French Revolution had shifted since 1800, and so far he had produced an outline with two names on it and a conviction that historians were arguing about something he could not quite see. Vanessa, who volunteered at the front desk between her immunology prerequisites, slid a request slip across the counter without looking up from her crossword.

"Basement or microfilm?" she asked.

"Basement," Evan said, though he didn't know what was in the basement. He only knew that the reading room upstairs, with its polished tables and its ceiling fans, made him feel like a fraud.

She led him down, past rolling shelves of municipal records, to a folder another library had deposited: reproductions of French Revolutionary prints, cheaply reissued for some centenary nobody remembered. He lifted the first one out with both hands. A festival on the Champ de Mars, drafted as a single vast crowd under a mountain, liberty seated at the peak, the whole composition pressing upward like something trying to be born. He had seen images like this in textbooks and had let them pass across his eyes as decoration. Now, with an essay due and nothing better, he stared until the print began to seem less like a picture of a festival than like an argument about what festivals were for.

Footsteps on the metal stairs. Anton came down two at a time, backpack riding high on his shoulders, and stopped when he saw the folder.

"Mr. He let you into the deposit?" Anton said. His voice was too even.

"He let you in first, apparently," Evan said.

"I've just been down here a couple of times." Anton set his bag on the far table, on top of it, and began pulling out notes in a fast, tidy stack, the way he did when he wanted to look busy. Vanessa, half visible at the bottom of the stairs, said nothing, but she did not go back up either.

Evan worked through the prints one by one. A liberty tree planted in a town square; a calendar with new month names; a poster of a festival with the text arranged in rays around a fixed point. Each one was doing something with symbols, with language, and the historians he'd read, the ones who counted grain prices and class alignments, had almost nothing to say about any of it. He was aware of Anton across the room, aware of the bag, aware of a small incipient tension he couldn't name. When Anton left to get water, the bag slumped sideways and a book slid halfway out: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution, Lynn Hunt, 1984, with a due-date slip showing three renewals in Anton's cramped print.

Evan turned it over and read the back flap, quietly, as much to himself as anyone. "Lynn Hunt's 1984 book turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution."

Anton stood at the bottom of the stairs, glass in hand, saying nothing. Vanessa looked at her shoes.

"You've had it since July," Evan said.

"I was going to tell you. After Friday." Friday was the deadline. Friday was also the day Mr. He, who coached the school's history prize, would read the top two submissions from their class, and they both knew which two. "It's a public archive book," Anton said. "I just got to it first."

"It was downstairs for a reason." Evan set the book on the table between them, spine up, and found he wasn't angry so much as recalibrating. "You were going to write the symbols essay and leave me the grain prices."

Anton didn't deny it. He sat down, finally, and after a while he said, "The grain prices matter. The festivals matter. I don't actually know which one explains more, and it's been keeping me up."

Evan laughed, once, surprised. He pulled a print toward him, the festival with the mountain, and set it beside the book. On a fresh sheet he wrote a question at the top: not which interpretation was right, but what each one could see that the other couldn't. Under it he wrote two columns, and left the bottom of the page open, because he did not yet know what belonged there.

Vanessa came the rest of the way down, sat, and turned the liberty tree print toward the light. "So are you two sharing it or fighting over it?"

"Both," Evan said, and pulled the mountain print back in front of him.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
On her third day at Millbrook High, Avery counted the hours she had spent with other human beings and arrived at a total of four, two of which had involved a fire drill. This seemed to her a solvable problem, the way a rubik's cube is solvable, tedious but with a known end state, and she liked problems with known end states. Back home she had been the one with a phone full of names, the girl who could walk into any lunchroom and find a table. Here she ate in the library stairwell, which smelled like glue and old rain, and told herself it was a temporary arrangement.

The temporary arrangement was interrupted on Thursday by a poster, slightly crooked, advertising the Astronomy Club, Thursdays after school, room 214, all welcome, no telescope required. Avery had no interest in astronomy. She did, however, have a research finding, which she had found at two in the morning in her old bedroom, cross-legged on a carpet that was already being packed into boxes. Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study had estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. She had written this on a sticky note and pressed it to her mirror like a prescription.

Ninety hours divided by weekly club meetings of roughly ninety minutes was an interminable number of Thursdays, something like sixty of them, more Thursdays than remained in her high school career if you subtracted holidays. But hours accumulated faster when people saw you in the hallway too, and at the vending machine, and in the miserable shared project for geography. The club was a seed crystal. She signed her name on the crooked poster and felt the small click of a plan beginning.

Room 214 contained six folding chairs, a tired model of Saturn, and a boy named Lincoln who was balancing a pencil on its tip with the concentration of a surgeon. "We meet at the same time every week," Avery said to him, by way of introduction, because she had decided honesty was more efficient than charm. "That's why I'm here." Lincoln let the pencil fall. "Most people come for the planet talk," he said. "You came for the attendance." He said it without judgment, which she appreciated, and then offered her a seat and half a bag of pretzels, which she also appreciated.

The club's president was a senior named Zara, who kept a notebook of observations and had, Avery discovered over three Thursdays, a genuine and slightly terrifying perspicacity about people. Zara noticed that Avery asked questions not about nebulae but about everyone's schedules. Zara noticed that Avery always arrived early and left late, stretching each meeting like taffy. On the fourth Thursday, Zara closed her notebook and said, "You're putting in hours. What are you building?" Avery considered lying, then didn't. "There was this study, 2018, Jeffrey Hall. Going from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. I'm running the experiment." Lincoln, from behind Saturn, said, "That is the least romantic thing I have ever heard," and Zara said, "It's the most honest," and both were true, and Avery noted, with interest, that being teased by people who knew your scheme was itself a kind of friendship, though the study had no row for it.

The Thursdays accumulated. There was the night the power went out and they held the meeting by phone flashlight, and the night Lincoln brought a telescope he'd borrowed from an uncle who did not exist, the telescope being a pair of binoculars and a paper towel tube. There was the afternoon Zara taught them constellations with such obvious delight that Avery, despite herself, was mesmerized, actually leaning forward, actually saying "wait, show me that one again," and losing forty minutes to the sky.

The twist arrived on a Tuesday in November, at the vending machine, where Zara was buying something called a Choco Wafer with visible reluctance. "Can I ask you something," Zara said. "Your 90 hours. Are you counting them? Like, actually counting." Avery hesitated, then admitted it: a note in her planner, updated weekly, currently at 47. Zara looked at the machine, pressed the button, and did not pick up her wafer. "Forty-nine," she said. "For me. Since September." Avery stared. "You've been counting too?" "Since the second club meeting," Zara said. "You told Lincoln your whole method in front of me on day one. I have perspicacity, not deafness. I thought, fine, we'll see who's right, the spreadsheet or the sky."

They stood in the hallway with the machine humming between them, two girls with parallel ledgers, and Avery understood that she could not say which had made the difference, the counting or the pretending not to count, the plan or the Thursdays that had stopped feeling like entries in one. Maybe the hours were the cause. Maybe they were only the clock a friendship happens to run on. "So who's ahead," Avery said. Zara finally took her wafer, tore it open, and offered half. "You're ahead by two hours," she said, "but I'm ahead by one Choco Wafer, and I know which one Lincoln values more."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Eva's mother had left for the evening with the subtlety of a departing army, which was to say she had kissed Eva twice, instructed her to text every hour, and promised not to litigate the terms of the curfew again once she returned. So the house belonged to Eva, and to the boy who was due in twenty minutes, and to the lasagna warming in the oven under foil that crinkled whenever she walked past. She had changed three times. The rejected shirts lay on the bed in a slumped heap, and she nudged them toward the donate pile, thinking that someone more destitute than she was could make good use of a shirt that had almost ruined her evening.

Kimberly had come over at four to supervise, and had stayed to supervise the supervising. "He's going to see your house," Kimberly said, standing in the doorway of Eva's room with the authority of a despot who had annexed this territory an hour ago. "Not the magazine house. This house, with the broken latch on the screen door and your dad's dragon collection."

"It's not a collection. It's four dragons."

"That's a collection."

Eva let it go, because Kimberly was partly right and entirely impossible, and because the doorbell was a real possibility now, a live wire in the wall. What Kimberly didn't know, what nobody knew, was the folded paper in Eva's back pocket, soft already from being refolded. She had found it in a magazine at the dentist's office two weeks ago and copied it onto a napkin, then onto real paper, then had sat at the kitchen table feeling faintly ridiculous, because the whole thing sounded like something you would find in the same waiting room as the napkin rings and the horoscopes.

At seven exactly the doorbell rang, and Eva went down the stairs at a pace she hoped read as casual, and opened the door on Daniel from her physics class, holding flowers he had clearly bought at the grocery store, since the price sticker was still on the plastic cone.

They ate at the kitchen table because the dining room felt like a courtroom, and for a while the lasagna carried them. He told her about his younger brother's obsession with weather balloons. She told him about the dragons. He laughed, actually laughed, and she felt something in her shoulders unlock, and she thought this might be easy, might be nothing, might be over before it started being anything at all.

Then the lasagna was gone, and the plates were pushed to the side, and the silence arrived like a third guest neither of them had invited. He stirred his empty glass with a straw that had nothing left to stir. She watched his eyes drift toward the window, toward the door, toward the jacket he had hung on the chair back, and she understood that people left through doors that were still closed, that he was half gone already, that in three minutes he would say something gracious about the food and the evening and the drive home, and she would say something gracious back, and that would be the whole story. The clock above the stove ticked. The foil in the oven made one soft settling sound. She put her hand in her back pocket, and the paper was there, and she thought, fine, fine, whatever happens.

"Do you know this thing," she said, "where in 1997 this psychologist, Arthur Aron, had pairs of strangers ask each other thirty-six questions, taking turns, and the questions got gradually more personal the deeper they went?" He stopped looking at the door. "And the pairs who did the questions ended up feeling closer than the pairs who just made small talk?"

"That's a real study?"

"That's a real study. I read it in a waiting room, which I admit is not the most romantic provenance." She unfolded the paper on the table between them, smoothing it flat. "We don't have to do all thirty-six. We could just trade harder questions until the lasagna wears off."

He pulled his jacket off the chair back and dropped it on the floor behind him, out of reach, which she noticed and did not comment on. "Okay," he said. "You first, or me?"

"You first," she said, turning the paper around so he could read the top question, and she watched him lean in, close enough that she could see the price sticker had left a faint ring of adhesive on his wrist where the flowers had rested.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
story:
Mya's cursor blinked at the top of an empty document titled "Common App Essay, Try 4." The prompt asked about a problem she wanted to solve, and for three days she had been obdurate about not writing the obvious thing, which was that her grandmother had been sent home from the hospital twice in one winter even though she could barely make it from her chair to the kitchen. Instead she had drafted essays about debate club and about learning to drive, and both had died on the page. Now it was ten at night, her door was shut, and her tea had gone cold beside the keyboard.

She opened a new tab instead and typed in a phrase she'd been carrying around since October: algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs. On the field trip to the health software company, the engineer with the lanyard had shown them a dashboard of patient risk scores, all little colored bars, and Yusuf, who never cared about looking smart in front of strangers, had put up his hand. "How do you know what the label really measures?" he'd asked. "Like, if you label somebody high risk, high risk of what?" The engineer had paused, and then, instead of the polished answer Mya expected, she'd told them about a 2019 study led by a researcher named Ziad Obermeyer. A widely used health-care algorithm in the US, she said, had underestimated how sick Black patients were, because it used how much patients had spent on medical care in the past as a stand-in for how sick they actually were.

Mya found the study now in three tabs at once: a summary, the abstract, a magazine piece. She read slowly, the way Ms. Oliveira had taught them to read primary sources in research seminar, checking each claim against the next telling of it. The numbers held. 2019, Obermeyer, the algorithm, the underestimation, the spending as the stand-in. She sat back. Nobody at the hospital had mentioned any algorithm to her grandmother. Nobody had mentioned a score. But someone, somewhere, had probably looked at a little colored bar and made a decision with it.

She pulled out her phone and called Yusuf, then added Ophelie when she picked up on the second ring. "You know how you asked that question on the field trip," Mya said. "Did you understand the answer?"

"Mostly," Yusuf said. His voice had the careful flatness he used when he was thinking. "The label was spending. But spending isn't the same thing as sickness. My dad spends almost nothing on doctors. He thinks going is a weakness. So a computer would look at him and think, this man is healthy."

"My grandma's the same," Mya said. "She didn't go in until she couldn't walk." On the screen, the study's abstract sat open, and she kept scrolling through it as they talked, as if the words might rearrange themselves into something less ugly. "So the machine wasn't told to do anything wrong. It was told to predict spending. And then everybody treated spending like sickness."

Ophelie's audio crackled; she was walking somewhere outside, wind moving across her microphone. "That's the part that scares me," she said. "There's no villain. You can't point at anyone. My mom says at least when a person discriminates against you, you can argue with them."

They were quiet for a moment, and Mya heard Ophelie's footsteps stop. "But wait," Ophelie said. "Is it the same thing, though? Discrimination, I mean. If a person does it, they intend it. If a machine does it, it just, inherits it. Like it inherits whatever was already true."

"It's inherited," Mya said. She turned the word over. "Like lineage. The machine inherits the pattern, and then the pattern gets passed down again every time it makes a decision." She typed the sentence into her empty document before she could lose it. The cursor finally had something to sit next to.

She emailed Ms. Oliveira at eleven, not expecting an answer, and got one at eleven twenty: a single line asking whether Mya wanted the study's methodology section for the seminar's current-events file, and a note that the college essay was a separate animal and could be ugly in its first draft. Mya smiled at that. She wrote back yes to the first part and nothing to the second, then reopened the essay document and stared at it. She wanted to write that the problem had a solution, that fixing the label would fix everything, and she did not believe it. Fixing the label was necessary and it was not enough. She did not know what came after, and she was tired of pretending that not knowing was a failure.

She thought about her grandmother in the recliner, oxygen line looped over her ears, watching Mya do homework at the kitchen table because she liked the company. In February, after the second discharge, a nurse had come to the house and fought for a referral, made calls from their hallway with her coat still on. That was a person resuscitating a decision the system had already let go cold. Mya wanted to be that kind of person, except with the machinery too, inside it, the part where the labels were chosen.

She typed a first line, deleted it, and typed it again. "The summer I turned seventeen, I learned that a hospital could look at my grandmother and see a number that was never meant to measure her at all." Outside her window a car passed, its lights sweeping the ceiling, and her phone buzzed with a message from Ophelie: a screenshot of a course listing, intro to data ethics, fall semester, and beneath it one line. "We could take it the same term."

"Save me a seat," Mya wrote back, and turned back to the screen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The rings hung above Ms. Rowe's television like a birthday banner that had stayed up too long, and Maelie had been staring at them since the opening ceremony began. Blue, yellow, black, green, red, on white. She had a plan for the evening, or half of one, which was to find her mother's flag in those colors, though her mother's flag was from a country that no longer existed in quite the same shape, which made the whole exercise feel like looking for a house that had been renovated twice since you left it.

"You're doing the thing," said Amira, elbow-deep in Ms. Rowe's popcorn bowl. "The squint. You look like you're trying to read the rings a secret."

"I'm looking for our colors. Green and white and a little red. There's green, there's red, there's white." Maelie tapped the screen, leaving a popcorn-butter fingerprint on a swimmer's face. "So technically we're in there. If the rings want us."

Eliot, folded into the armchair with the sullen posture of someone who had lost an argument about which channel to watch, snorted without unfolding. "The rings don't want anything. They're a logo. Pierre de Coubertin designed them in 1913 and someone in a meeting decided they'd test well." He said it the way he said most things, as though the world were a contrivance assembled by people less clever than he was, and Maelie privately thought that half his cynicism was a costume he'd put on in tenth grade and that had since ossified, like a bone set wrong.

"He picked the colors on purpose," she said. "Every national flag of the time has at least one of them. Including the white background. That's the whole trick. Nobody's left out." She was quoting, more or less, from a folded page in her back pocket, and this was the other half of her plan.

Amira's mother had texted her an hour ago: an old friend of Maelie's mother had written a letter, an actual paper letter, and it had arrived at their apartment addressed to Maelie. Amira had photographed it. She produced her phone now, under the table, as if they were passing contraband. "You can read it but you can't cry at Ms. Rowe's, she just shampooed the rug."

The letter was from a woman Maelie had never met, her mother's old teacher, and it said that her mother, at seventeen, had sat on a roof during the qualifiers for a Games she would never attend and had pointed at the flag colors on her own scarf and said, "One day somebody will have to make room for all of us at once." The woman wrote that she had never forgotten it, and that when the rings came on her television she thought of that scarf, and that she hoped Maelie would forgive a stranger for saying so.

Maelie read it twice. The second time she did not cry, mostly because Amira was watching her with the vigilant tenderness of a person holding a fire extinguisher.

Upstairs, the game they had actually gathered for had started, the one Ms. Rowe's nephew was playing in, and the adults were shouting at the screen with a sincerity that made Eliot wince. Ms. Rowe came down with a tray of cups and caught Maelie looking at the rings again.

"You remind me of my sister," Ms. Rowe said, setting down a cup in front of her with the firmness of a woman who did not permit refusals. "She used to say the rings were a promise. I used to say they were a billboard. We argued about it for forty years and I still don't know who won."

"That's not how arguments work," Eliot said.

"That's exactly how arguments work, sweetheart. Nobody wins, you just get old together." She patted his shoulder on her way back up, and he pretended to be wounded by it, and failed.

The noise overhead doubled. Someone had scored, or almost scored, and Maelie could hear her father's voice crack on a shout, which he would deny later. She looked at the rings, then at the letter, then at Eliot, who was now leaning forward despite himself because the replay was genuinely good.

"Okay, you're right that it's a logo," she said. "It's a contrivance, fine. But it's a contrivance that has to include everybody to work. That's not nothing. Somebody sat down and made a thing that couldn't exclude anyone on purpose. Even if the reason was publicity, the effect is you can find yourself in it. My mom's colors are in there. Amira's are in there. Yours are, what, blue and white?"

"And red," Eliot admitted. "Fine. It's an inclusive billboard. A very well-engineered piece of propaganda for the idea that propaganda can be nice." He gestured at the screen, where the athletes were milling in their conflicting flags. "I don't hate it. That's my concession. I've changed my mind from hating it to not hating it, and I'd like credit."

"You'll get a certificate," said Amira. "Laminated."

Maelie folded the letter along its creases and put it in her back pocket next to the page with the rings on it, one piece of paper about a scarf, one about a design from 1913, and it occurred to her that both of them were true at once and neither settled anything, and that this was probably fine. Upstairs her father screamed something about a penalty. She took the stairs two at a time, and Eliot, grumbling, followed, and Amira carried the popcorn.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The festival had taken over the river park by ten in the morning, and by noon the smell of grilled lamb and fried dough had merged into a single sweetness that hung over everything. Ryan carried a folded newspaper, the Greek one his grandfather still had delivered though he could barely see to read it, because the heritage booth at the far end had offered a deal: read one short article aloud, summarize it in your own words, and you could take a pastry from the tray without paying. The article was about the festival itself, three column inches announcing a children's dance troupe and an evening concert.

"Read it to us," Jaiden said, falling into step beside him. Jaiden had been voluble since the parking lot, narrating every stall they passed, the accordion player, the woman selling honey in mismatched jars. "Do the whole thing in Greek. I want to hear what you sound like."

Ryan spread the paper on the counter of the booth while the old man behind it, small and unhurried, turned the pastry tray so the best ones faced out. Dimitri arrived a moment later with three cups of thick coffee and said nothing, which for Dimitri was a kind of greeting. Ryan began at the first word and moved through the article the way he had moved through every assigned page since September, left to right, word by word, mouthing the unfamiliar ones.

He was four lines in when he realized he had passed the thing he needed. The concert, he knew, was tonight, but the article gave a specific hour and he had drifted past it. He went back to the beginning and started again, slower this time, and Jaiden made an exasperated noise and put his hand flat on the page.

"What are you doing?"

"Finding the time of the concert. I need it for the summary."

"You don't read the whole article for that. That's scanning. You scan for one thing, a number, a name. Skimming is different, that's reading fast for the general idea." Jaiden tapped the column. "Scan for the number, then skim the rest so you know what it's about. You're doing neither. You're crawling."

Ryan looked at the gray wall of print and understood, with a small inward shift, that he had been reading everything in his life at one speed. His grandfather, who used to sit at the kitchen table with this same paper, had never seemed to crawl through it. He turned the pages like a man shuffling cards, pausing where something caught him. Ryan had assumed that was a lifetime of fluency. Now he wondered if it was partly method, a choosing of speeds.

He put his finger at the top of the article and let his eyes drop straight down, not reading, only looking for the shape of a numeral, and there it was, a time, and beside it the name of the church hall. Then, having that, he skimmed, letting the words come at him in groups, and the article opened like something unfolding. The troupe was from the city, the concert was a fundraiser, the whole piece was three sentences wearing the costume of six. He said as much aloud, in English, and the old man waited. Ryan took a breath and gave the summary again, in Greek, halting, wrong stress on one word, right on another. The old man corrected nothing. He lifted a pastry with a small paper square and set it in front of Ryan, then set out two more.

"Extenuate," Dimitri said finally, his first word in an hour, and both of them looked at him. "Your summary. You made the article sound better than it was. You extenuated it." He drank his coffee. "It was three sentences of nothing and you made it sound like an event."

Mr. Campbell, who had taught all three of them chemistry two years ago and now stood at the next booth buying bread, glanced over at the sound of the word. He raised his eyebrows at Ryan, a small salute, and moved on. Ryan ate half the pastry and thought about what Dimitri had said, because it was true and because he was not sure it was a criticism. The article was slight, but the concert was real, and tonight people he had known his whole life would stand in a church hall and sing. Choosing what to amplify was not the same as lying. Or maybe it was, a little, and the difference depended on something he could not yet name.

"Six words," Jaiden said. "Your whole summary in six words. Children dance, church hall, eight o'clock."

"Seven," said the old man, without looking up from his tray, and slid the last pastry toward him.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
The hardware store smelled like cut pine and machine oil, and Benjamin stood at the register trying not to touch anything. Ms. Wong, the owner, slid a form across the counter and uncapped a pen for him. She had hired him on the strength of one conversation and his mother's recommendation, which he suspected counted more than the conversation. The pay was minimum wage, the hours were Saturdays and two evenings, and the work was mostly carrying things heavier than he was used to carrying.

"You'll want to read that before you sign," Ms. Wong said, and turned to price a bucket of nails, which had somehow been shelved under plumbing.

He read it. It was short. Nowhere did it promise him anything, and nowhere did it ask him for anything either, except that he show up and do the work. There was no term of employment, no contract length, nothing about severance or notice. He signed anyway, because he wanted the money for a laptop before college, and because it was the first job anyone had offered him.

By the third Saturday he understood why the last boy had left. The work was not hard so much as endless: hoses to coil, paint cans nobody had alphabetized, a customer who wanted to argue about the veracity of a receipt from 2019. Ms. Wong was fair but exacting, and when the Saturdays stretched into eleven hours during the spring rush, Benjamin began composing elaborate resignation speeches in his head during his lunch break, most of them involving the phrase "I regret to inform you." He had read somewhere that leaving without two weeks' notice made you unemployable forever, a fact that had settled in his chest with a kind of visceral dread.

He brought it up with Markus, who worked at the grocery store across the lot and who was eating fries on the loading dock behind the hardware store like it was his personal terrace.

"Notice is a courtesy, not a law," Markus said, chewing. "Most jobs here are at-will. The employer can end it any time, for any reason that's not illegal, and the worker can quit the same way. That's what at-will means."

"So I could just not show up Monday."

"I mean, you'd be a jerk. But they could fire you on a Monday too. Nobody's suing anybody over a Saturday kid." Markus waved a fry. "You want to litigate a hose-coiling position, be my guest."

Benjamin laughed, but the information rearranged something. It was not that he wanted to quit without warning; it was that the fear had been shaped like a law, and now it was shaped like a choice. He turned it over for most of a week. On one side was the principle his mother had raised him with, that you finish what you start and leave a place better than you found it. On the other was the plain fact that the arrangement bound neither party, that Ms. Wong would not hesitate to let him go if the spring rush ended, and that pretending otherwise was a kind of dishonesty about what he'd signed. Neither argument won. What he settled on was smaller and more practical: he would give notice, but not because he owed it. Because he might want a reference, and because eleven hours was too many, and those were reasons he could defend out loud.

The next Saturday, between customers, he found Ms. Wong at the paint mixer.

"Spring rush runs through June," he said. "I can do eight-hour Saturdays until then, but eleven is more than I can do well."

She let the mixer run its cycle before she answered. "The boy before you asked for fewer hours by text."

"I'm asking in person."

"That's why you're still here and he isn't." She shook the can of off-white, popped the lid, and checked the color against the swatch taped to the register. "Eight hours. Clock out at five. And reorganize the hose wall while you still feel like negotiating."

He went back to the hose wall, which had been waiting for him all day, patient as a debt.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
The printmaking studio smelled of ink and dish soap, and Hudson had claimed the corner table since the first Monday of the session, guarding it with a drawstring bag of brushes like a dog with a bone. Ten artworks around one theme, that was the assignment Mr. Shin had set on the first day, plus an artist's statement, all due at the Friday exhibition. Hudson had eleven pieces already, which was the problem, because eleven meant he had to choose, and choosing meant deciding what the portfolio was actually about.

His theme, as he'd written it on the butcher paper taped above his table, was "Water." He had a lino print of a drowned bicycle, a watercolor of his grandmother's kitchen sink, a collagraph of rain on a windshield. The pieces were good. He knew they were good because Alena kept borrowing them to show people at other tables, which was flattering until Odin leaned over during lunch and said, "You know this isn't a theme, right? It's a subject. A theme would be like, grief, or memory. Water's just a thing that's wet."

Hudson had been peevish about that for most of an afternoon, snapping his brayer against the glass plate harder than the ink required, until Alena sat down across from him with her own portfolio spread out and said, "He's not wrong, but he's not right either. My theme is 'doors,' and half my pieces don't have doors in them. The theme is what you're thinking about, not what you're drawing." She was making a series about her parents' divorce, though she'd never said so in those words, and every piece had a doorway in it, half open or half shut, and Hudson had understood the divorce part without being told, which seemed like proof that she was doing something he wasn't.

That night, in the bunk above Odin's, he started the artist's statement, because it was due Thursday and he wanted it out of the way. He wrote three sentences. "The artist is interested in water as a subject of memory. The artist uses printmaking and watercolor. The artist grew up near a reservoir." He read it back and felt the peculiar flatness of it, like a museum label for a stranger, and he couldn't decide whether that was professional or just false.

He took the draft to Mr. Shin the next morning, mostly to have something to hand in. Mr. Shin read it leaning against the supply cabinet, one ankle crossed over the other, and then said, "Say 'I.'" That was all he said. He handed the paper back and went to help a girl whose collagraph was peeling at the edges.

Hudson sat with it. He crossed out "the artist" and wrote "I am interested in water" and then stopped, because the sentence wasn't true. He wasn't interested in water. He was interested in the reservoir by his grandfather's old house, the one his grandfather had been evicted from when the county flooded the valley, the one Hudson had swum in all through middle school without knowing there was a town under him until his mother mentioned it offhand one summer, driving past, the way you mention that a house used to stand where a parking lot is now. Water wasn't his theme. Disappearance was. Water was just how disappearance happened, where he came from.

He rewrote the statement in first person, all of it, and the act of writing "I" over and over did something strange and clarifying, because every time the word appeared he had to check whether he meant it. "I make prints of things that were submerged." "I never met the people who lived there." "I don't know if remembering them is mine to do." That last sentence he underlined once, then left alone. He thought about his school art classes, which had inculcated in him a certain nervousness about the word "I," a training toward the passive voice, as though a person could make things without being a person making them. Alena had never been trained that way. Her whole portfolio was an argument that ontology and autobiography could be the same thing, that what a thing was and who she was could share a page.

At the Friday exhibition he hung nine pieces, not ten, having cut the weakest two and pulled one from a folder he'd been hiding, a drypoint of the reservoir's surface with a faint grid of streets showing through, ghostlike, beneath. His statement was pinned beside it, still in first person, still ending on the sentence about not knowing whether remembering was his to do. Odin read it with his hands in his pockets and said, "This is better." Alena read it twice and didn't say anything, which Hudson understood as the highest available review.

His parents arrived late, his mother with sunscreen still on her nose, and stood in front of the drypoint for a long moment. "I never told you the street names," she said. "How did you get the streets right?"

Hudson looked at the print, at the grid he had copied from a county map in the library, at the water he had layered over it with the flat of a burnisher. "I looked them up," he said. "I can show you the map."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum.
story:
Claire set her notebook on the kitchen table and opened it to the page her calculus teacher had marked with a red arrow and nothing else. The problem asked for the area under a curve between zero and four, and beneath the curve was drawn the long, slender symbol she was supposed to use, like a stretched S lying on its side, wearing small numbers at its top and bottom like hats. She had copied six examples from the board that afternoon, but when she tried the seventh alone, her pen stopped above the paper and hovered there.

Leyla arrived at four with her history textbook under one arm and a bag of clementines. She sat down across from Claire, peeled a clementine in one long spiral, and began reading aloud from an essay prompt about sectarian divisions in seventeenth-century Europe, pausing every few sentences to complain that the textbook expected her to contextualize everything without ever explaining what counted as context. "Like I'm supposed to know which details matter," she said. "Meanwhile you get numbers. Numbers have answers."

"Numbers have answers if you know what the symbols mean," Claire said. "This one, I don't even know what it's called. Mr. Reyes never said. He just drew it and started computing." She traced the shape in the margin of her notes, the tall thin curve leaning right, and thought it looked like something half-erased, or something that had started as one letter and been pulled like taffy into another.

Leyla leaned over to look. "It's like a funky S," she said, and went back to her essay, underlining phrases about religious conflict in the German states, and after a while the two of them worked in the kind of quiet that only happens at a kitchen table in late afternoon, with the refrigerator humming and the light going amber on the wall.

Claire couldn't leave the symbol alone. She took out her phone, meaning only to check a homework site, but instead she typed the question that had been bothering her, why the integral sign looks like a stretched letter, and the first result was a scan of an old notebook page. In the corner of a sheet dated 1675, in ink gone brown, Gottfried Leibniz had written the symbol for the first time. The site said he based it on an elongated letter s, because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum. She read the line twice, then set the phone face down on the table so the fact wouldn't slide away from her the way formulas did.

An infinite sum. She looked again at the curve on her page, the region beneath it shaded lightly in the textbook's printing. She had been treating the shaded part as one solid thing to be measured, like the floor of a room, and the answer as a number you arrived at through a mechanical trick, the antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints. But Leibniz, apparently, had seen something else entirely: infinitely many infinitely thin slices, each one added to the next, s for sum, stretched out long because the summing never stopped. Two completely different pictures of the same shape, and the formula, which had felt like arbitrary procedure that morning, suddenly looked like a bridge between them. The mechanical trick computed what the infinite adding would add up to, if anyone could actually finish adding forever.

She tested the idea on her problem, drawing rectangles under the curve, ten of them, then imagining ten thousand, each one so thin it was almost nothing, almost nothing times an almost infinite count. Her pen moved without her quite deciding, and she computed the antiderivative, plugged in four, plugged in zero, subtracted, and got a number with a clean fraction in it. She checked it against the answer in the back of the book and it matched, and she sat back in the chair with the particular looseness that comes after something difficult has gone right.

"It's an S," she said to Leyla. "For sum. This guy Leibniz, in 1675, he made it an elongated s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum." Leyla looked up from her essay, and Claire pointed at the page. "So the symbol isn't just notation somebody invented to be difficult. It's a picture of the idea. It's doing the thinking inside the writing."

Leyla came around the table and studied the curve, the rectangles, the answer circled twice. "So you're telling me math has meaning embedded in the shapes."
