She said it in the tone she used for the history textbook, half skeptical, half delighted. "Great. Now I have to contextualize Leibniz too." She tapped the prompt about the German states. "He's from around there, right? Same century as my essay." Claire said she honestly didn't know, that she knew only what the scan had shown her, one notebook page and one sentence about a letter, and that she wasn't sure yet how much of what she'd just felt was real understanding and how much was the artifice of a good story about a symbol. It was possible the feeling of insight would fade by tomorrow and she'd be back to following steps without seeing anything. She was willing to find out.

They worked until the light turned gray and Leyla packed up her essay, still muttering about context. After she left, Claire stayed at the table. She wrote the symbol once more at the top of a clean page, slowly, the way Leibniz must have written it the first time, and then she drew the curve again and began another problem, one the teacher hadn't assigned, from a section they hadn't reached yet.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: Bigger samples help less than people expect: doubling a random sample from 1,000 to 2,000 people shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point.
story:
The poll had Gavin up by six, and Shaelyn had texted him the screenshot before he'd even parked his bike: "asked 1,000 likely voters, margin of error plus or minus three." He read it twice at the red light on Marsh Street, then a third time in the campaign office doorway, where Graysen was already stacking chairs.

"We're doing it," Graysen said. "Six points, Gav. That's the race, right there."

Gavin had spent the whole walk home turning the numbers over the way his mother turned a knob of butter to see whether it was soft enough. By the time he sat down at the dinner table, the paper was still folded in his jacket pocket, and his father was ladling soup into bowls while his mother argued cheerfully with Gavin's little brother about whether peas had feelings.

"They have a phenotype," Gavin said, mostly to rescue the peas. "That's just what they look like. You can't hurt a phenotype." His brother accepted this with the gravity of a nine-year-old lawyer and went back to stabbing his fork at the evidence.

"So the debate's Thursday," his father said, in the tone he used when he wanted to be asked more but would never say so. "You two been out knocking doors all week. I saw you on Culver."

"Phones, mostly," Gavin said. "The campaign does polls. There was one today." He laid his phone flat on the table between the bread basket and his brother's milk, screen up, and watched his father squint at it.

"Plus or minus three," his father read. "That's good, isn't it? Six-point lead."

"Could be three," Gavin said. "Could be nine. That's what the margin of error means. It's not a fudge, it's just what a thousand people can tell you."

His brother reached for the phone and Gavin moved it out of range without looking, an old reflex. His mother spooned more soup into his bowl before he'd touched the first serving, which was her way of saying she knew he'd been skipping lunch on canvassing days.

"Graysen wants to double the calls," he went on. "He thinks if we get to two thousand people, we can, like, nail it down. Make the poll accurate. He's trying to organize a weekend blitz."

"And you don't think it works?"

"I looked it up this afternoon. In the office, on Mr. Yoon's laptop, while everyone was at the rally." Their neighbor had let him in to wait out the rain and had gone back to grading without a word, sliding the laptop across the kitchen table like a man setting out a place mat. "Doubling the sample from a thousand to two thousand shrinks the margin of error by about one point. That's all. All those extra calls, all weekend, and you go from plus or minus three to plus or minus two."

His father set down his spoon. "One point for a thousand more calls?"

"One point." Gavin said it flatly, the way Mr. Yoon had said nothing at all while Gavin stared at the chart on the screen. It had felt like a joke at first, the kind where the math was hiding something, and he'd checked the number three times before the rain stopped.

His mother leaned in. "So what do you tell Graysen? He's so excited about the blitz."

"I don't know yet." Gavin tore a piece of bread he didn't want. "I told him tonight and he tried to expostulate. Like, full courtroom mode. 'Every call counts, every voter matters.' Which is true when you're turning out votes. It's just not true for the poll." He paused, working the bread into a ball. "They're two different things wearing the same T-shirt. Calling voters to remind them to vote, that's worth everything. Calling them to make the number prettier, that's mostly nothing."

His brother, with the insouciant confidence of someone who had never once been asked to be useful, said, "Just do both."

"Thank you," Gavin's mother said, pointing her spoon at him as though he had delivered a ruling.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Gavin said. "A six-point lead with a three-point margin, that still means he's probably ahead. Probably. And a two-point margin would feel safer, even if it costs us the whole weekend we could spend knocking on actual doors. So it's not that the blitz is crazy. It's that it buys the wrong thing." He looked at the folded paper still poking out of his jacket, the walk sheets with forty names on each, and then at his cooling soup. "I keep trying to make the number tell me what to do, and it won't. It just sits there being honest about what it doesn't know."

His father reached over and slid the breadboard closer to Gavin's elbow, the way he did when he thought somebody was talking too much to eat. Gavin took the hint. For a while there was only the sound of spoons and his brother narrating the peas' final moments.

After dinner he texted Graysen from the front steps, thumbs slow: one point, not three. Not a reason to skip the blitz if the calls remind people to vote. But not a reason to think we've won, either.

The reply came while he was still watching the three dots pulse. "so what do we do saturday"

Gavin looked up. Across the street, Mr. Yoon's kitchen light was on, the laptop closed on his table like a book somebody had finished.

"We knock doors," he typed. "Bring the good clipboards. I'll carry the list."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
story:
The morning of her peer-education session, Amelia stood at the picnic table behind the infirmary, sorting condoms and pamphlets into paper bags, and discovered that someone had absconded with the entire box of dental dams. She counted twice. Sixty pamphlets on consent, forty on contraception, two boxes of condoms, and a gap where the dental dams should have been. The session was in ninety minutes. She went looking for Kira, who had been her co-trainee through the whole certification weekend in June, and found her at the lake, skipping stones with a boy from the sail barn.

"You have to help me," Amelia said. "Someone took the dental dams."

"Maybe the infirmary just ran out," Kira said, not turning around. Her stone skipped four times before it sank into the pelagic gray of the morning water, though the lake was hardly an ocean; Amelia had always thought the word was too grand for it, and Kira used it anyway, every summer, the way she used most words, loosely and with confidence.

"Mr. Addo ordered them special," Amelia said. "And my whole session is about, you know, the full picture. Consent, contraception, where to get tested. If I skip a piece, the ninth graders will notice."

Kira finally turned. "Can we talk after? There's something I actually need to ask you." She glanced at the boy, who had the grace to study the horizon, and Amelia understood that whatever it was, it was private, and that Kira had chosen her.

They found the dental dams an hour later in the arts shed, hidden behind the glitter, apparently taken as a joke by a cabin of fifteen-year-olds who had then lost their nerve. Amelia didn't lecture them. She handed each of them a pamphlet instead and said, "Read this, and if you have questions on Thursday, I'm the one at the front of the room." The tallest of them turned the pamphlet over twice, as if checking for a trick, and put it in his back pocket, which Amelia decided to count as a win.

The session itself began badly. One of the ninth graders, Jade, had a newspaper article folded in her pocket, printed from her phone, about a law in another country, and she wanted to know why the age of consent there was different from here, because her grandmother in Ohio insisted it was one number and the article said another. "Which one is right?" Jade asked, arms crossed, and half the room leaned in, because it was the first question that smelled like an argument.

"I don't know which one is right," Amelia said, "because there isn't one right one. It's different by country, and in the US it even differs between states, and in a lot of places it falls somewhere between sixteen and eighteen." She had learned this during her training, had written it on an index card and then thrown the card away because it seemed like the kind of thing she'd never need, and now here it was, needed. "So your grandmother might be right about Ohio, and the article might be right about that country, and both of you could still be wrong about a third place."

"That's a terrible system," Jade said.

"Maybe," Amelia said. "But knowing it varies is the important part. It means you actually have to find out the law where you are. You can't just assume." She felt the room shift, a small loosening, the way it did when a fact stopped being a lecture and became a tool. They moved on to contraception, to the clinic forty minutes away by bus where testing was free and confidential, to what the word confidential actually covered and what it didn't. Jade took notes in surprisingly small handwriting.

Afterward, Kira found her at the picnic table, repacking the paper bags. "So what I wanted to ask," Kira said, and then stopped, and started again. "Thursday. Could you not mention that I came to you? If I come to you." She was picking at the edge of a pamphlet, and Amelia watched her do it and said nothing, because the silence was the answer Kira needed first.

"Whenever you're ready, it's just us," Amelia said at last. "And I'll go over the clinic stuff, the bus, all of it. Not in the session. Just us." She handed Kira one of the remaining paper bags, the one with the pamphlet about consent, the one with the clinic's address printed on the back, and Kira held it against her chest with both hands, like something she was guarding rather than carrying, and the two of them walked up the hill toward the mess hall together, Kira matching her step for step without being asked.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted '7 percent words, 38 percent tone, 55 percent face' rule came from experiments on conveying feelings, and he said it does not apply to all communication.
story:
Austin sat on his grandfather's porch swing with his phone in one hand and a printed application in the other, the paper already soft at the corners from being folded and refolded. The interview at the garden center was at ten the next morning, his first ever, and every answer he rehearsed came out sounding like a customs declaration. He had read, somewhere in the scroll of a night, that only seven percent of communication was words, thirty-eight percent was tone, and fifty-five percent was the face, which meant he could stop torturing himself over phrasing and simply practice looking like a person who knew what he was doing. That math felt like mercy.

Inside, his grandfather's kitchen smelled of coffee kept warm too long, and the window over the sink held the reflection of the backyard where the swing chain had rusted a brown stain down the siding. Austin's grandmother set a plate of sliced peaches in front of him without being asked, the way she had since he was small, and asked him to say his answer about customer service again, slower this time. When he finished she said, "That was nice, dear," and he could not tell whether the softness in her voice was approval or pity, which seemed to prove his point about tone.

He called Kenley from the porch after dinner, the cicadas so loud he had to press the phone flat to his ear. Kenley was the one who had first shared the statistic, in a group chat, with a string of fire emojis, back when they were both applying to the same handful of jobs. Austin told him the plan: forget the sentences, drill the face in the bathroom mirror, walk in with eyebrows that conveyed competence. There was a pause on the line long enough for him to hear Kenley's television in the background. "You know I looked it up after I sent that," Kenley said. "The numbers came from a psychologist named Albert Mehrabian, and his experiments were about conveying feelings, not everything. He said himself it doesn't apply to all communication."

Austin argued for a while, because it was easier than admitting he had built a whole evening on a misreading. He said that a job interview was basically feelings, that the manager would decide within seconds whether she liked him. Kenley said maybe, but she would also ask why he left his last job, and no amount of eyebrow would answer that. Then Kenley's mother called him for dinner and the call ended without a resolution, which felt appropriate.

That night Austin could not sleep in the guest room with its vestigial trundle bed still pushed beneath the frame, left over from a childhood he had technically outgrown. He lay sweating under a quilt his grandmother insisted on regardless of the season, and he kept circling back to the summer he was eleven, when he had lied to this same grandfather about breaking the porch railing and his grandfather had known instantly, not from the words, which were careful, but from something in Austin's face that no eleven-year-old could govern. He remembered being sent to sit on the steps until he was ready to tell the truth, and how the truth, once spoken, had taken less effort than the lie.

At two in the morning he got up and went down the hall to his grandfather's old computer, the monitor's fan whirring like a small appliance, and looked up Mehrabian himself. It was all there in Kenley's shape: the experiments about conveying feelings, the numbers everyone quoted, the man's own insistence that the rule did not apply to all communication. Austin sat with his hands on the warm keyboard and thought about the two truths he was holding. The face mattered; he knew that from the railing. And the words mattered; he knew that from every moment the truth had been easier than the circumlocution. Neither one could underwrite the whole interview on its own, and what remained uncertain was the ratio, which no one on the internet seemed to agree about anyway.

In the morning his grandfather drove him, the truck smelling of fertilizer and the coffee his grandmother had sent along in a thermos that had outlasted three presidencies. In the parking lot Austin sat for a minute with his hand on the door. He had practiced the answers out loud on the porch until the words stopped feeling borrowed, and he had also practiced looking up from his shoes, because a person who meant what he said generally looked like it. It was not a formula. It was more like the difference between the lying summer and the truth-telling one, except this time there was nothing to confess, only a desire to work near plants and be paid for it.

He checked his reflection in the truck's side mirror, straightened a collar that did not need straightening, and went in. The manager, a woman with dirt permanently under her thumbnails, asked her first question, and Austin looked at her and began, "Sure, I can answer that."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
story:
Lea sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop open to Mr. Haddad's biology notes and, beside it, her half-edited video from the weekend, the one Georgia had filmed of her and Jersey skating the flooded quarry road. She had a test in two days on how DNA gets copied into protein, and she had been staring at the same paragraph so long the words had started to look like wallpaper.

"This is hopeless," she said to the room, and dragged her cursor along the timeline anyway. In the footage she and Jersey kept messing up the same turn, so there were eleven bad takes in a row, then one where she actually landed it. She highlighted a bad take, cut it, and watched the two good pieces on either side knit themselves together into something that looked like it had always been one smooth run.

She looked at the biology notes. Then back at the timeline. Then at the notes again.

"Wait," she said out loud, and called Jersey, because Jersey had already gone through the chapter and claimed it was easy, which Lea suspected was a lie. "Okay, so the DNA gets copied into RNA, right, in the nucleus. But the chapter keeps saying the RNA that comes out the other side isn't the same length as what went in."

"That's the introns," Jersey said, mouth full of something. "Introns get cut out."

"Cut out of the new RNA," Lea said slowly, watching her timeline as she said it, watching the bad take lift away from the track. "And then the pieces that are left, the exons, get spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus." She said it twice more, once to Jersey and once to the ceiling, and it was like the paragraph had been a bad take itself and now it was one smooth run. She was doing to RNA what she was doing to the video: cutting out what didn't belong and joining the good parts so the finished thing could go out into the world.

She worked through the rest of it that way. Transcription was the filming, all the raw material, the eleven failures and the one success stacked in a row. Translation was the final export, the version people would actually see, the protein. What she liked, and what she kept turning over while she ate dinner with her mother and half-listened to a story about the boreal forest her mother was reading for a book club, was that the cell did this deliberately. It wasn't a mistake being cleaned up. The cutting was part of making the thing at all.

She texted Georgia about it at ten. Georgia wrote back, "ok nerd," and then, a minute later, "wait explain the intron thing again," and Lea typed it out and found she could, without the notes, without Jersey, without the video playing beside her. It held on its own.

The next morning she came downstairs early and found Mr. Haddad's review session already started in her kitchen, which was to say her mother had invited him in when he came by about the neighbour thing, and he was standing at the counter with coffee. "I hear you've been splicing," he said.

"Like film editing," Lea said. "Cut out the introns, splice the exons, and only then does the mRNA ship out."

Mr. Haddad smiled into his cup. There was a question she still couldn't answer, though, the one that had kept her up after Georgia's texts went quiet: whether the cell's version of editing was fixed, every cut predetermined by the sequence, or whether there was choice in it. It felt like a question about determinism, honestly, about whether anything that made something new could do otherwise, and she didn't have the machinery yet to know. She had a test in two days that would not ask it. She took a banana from the bowl and said, "Can I show you something on my laptop before school? It'll take four minutes."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Xavier cleared the living room of its furniture by four o'clock, dragging the coffee table to the hallway and stacking the chairs against the bookshelf so the carpet became a stage. His mother had agreed to underwrite the whole production, which meant eleven dollars for masking tape and a printed stack of scripts, and she kept saying it was nothing, which only made him tally it more carefully. The one-act was due at the community theatre showcase in nine days, and until this morning he had thought directing meant telling people how to say their lines. He no longer thought that.

Hafsa arrived first with a shoebox under her arm. She knelt on the carpet, opened it, and set out a grid of masking tape squares, then placed a coin on each square. "Mathis told me you had no idea what blocking was," she said. "He said you kept saying the actors would just figure out where to stand."

"I said they'd figure it out naturally."

"That's what a person says who has never watched two actors stand in the same spot for four minutes." She slid a coin two squares forward. "This is Mathis in the opening. This is me. Watch." She moved the coins through the first scene, a slow circling that looked, even in miniature, like a negotiation.

He watched the coins and understood something without being able to say it yet, which was the most irritating kind of understanding. When Mathis arrived, dropping his bag by the door, Xavier asked him where the word had come from, and Mathis shrugged and said it went back to nineteenth-century directors like W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. "So the coins are the block," Hafsa said, "and we're the model stage, except the model stage is your living room."

They rehearsed. Xavier discovered that Hafsa took direction as an offer, tilting her head at a note and trying it three ways, while Mathis took each note as a verdict, and the same words that freed one tightened the other. He learned to say "walk toward the window on that line" instead of "be sadder," and both of them improved, which felt like a trick he had performed on himself. Twice the tape came up off the carpet. Twice he knelt and pressed it back down.

The confounder was the doorway. His mother passed through it four times in the first hour, once with laundry, once to say the oven timer would go off, and the actors' eyes tracked her every time, breaking the rectangle of the scene. Xavier taped a fourth wall across the doorway, a long strip at waist height, and told them to play it as though nothing existed beyond it. Mathis laughed and said the tape was impecunious theatre at its finest, but he stopped watching the doorway, and his whole body settled into the scene as if the wall were real.

Later, while the other two ate leftovers in the kitchen, Xavier sat alone on the carpet with the coins. He thought about the year before, when he had auditioned for the school play and not been cast, and how he had told everyone, including himself, that he was over it. He was not sure he was over it, and he was not sure whether directing was what he wanted or what he had landed on because it was near the thing he wanted. Both could be true. He arranged the coins on their grid and moved them through the final scene, the one where the two characters decide to leave, and found that no arrangement he tried made the ending land.

When Hafsa came back in with a glass of water, she stood over him and watched him slide her coin toward the edge of the tape. "That's not where I'd go," she said.

"Where would you go?"

She knelt, picked up her coin, and set it dead center, equidistant from Mathis's coin and the doorway, facing neither. Xavier looked at it for a long moment. Then he picked up Mathis's coin and placed it behind hers, both of them still, the whole ending changed and nothing yet decided.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp, which applies to every F in the piece unless an accidental changes it.
story:
The community centre keyboard room smelled of instant noodles and floor polish, and Nevaeh had until Friday to finish a melody that did not yet exist. Ms. Cheung had said sixteen bars, chord changes, proper notation, and then she had said the part that kept Nevaeh awake: "You'll hear each other's work played out loud, so write something you can stand behind." That was four days ago. Tonight was Tuesday, and what Nevaeh had was a tune in her head that vanished whenever she picked up the pencil.

Charlie was already at the good keyboard, the one by the window, playing the same four bars over and over with an expression of deep suspicion. Sahana sat on the radiator cover with a theory workbook open on her knees, highlighting things apparently at random. Nevaeh spread her staff paper on the folding table and hummed her opening phrase, the one that had sounded so certain in the shower that morning. On paper it wandered. She wrote a G chord under the first bar, then a C under the fifth, and stopped, because she could hear that the second chord wanted something from the melody that the melody was not giving.

"It's flat," she said to nobody, then to Charlie, "does this sound flat to you?" She played her five bars slowly. Charlie listened with his eyes closed, which he claimed helped but which mostly looked like napping. "The third bar," he said. "The second note. It's not bad, it's just not the note you think it is."

Nevaeh looked at bar three. She had written an F natural, or rather she had written an F with nothing next to it, because in her head the note had been the bright one, the one that leaned toward G. She counted the sharps at the start of her staff. One. She had chosen G major for a reason she could not entirely defend, something about it feeling open, and the single sharp in the signature sat there at the beginning of every line like a small promise she had forgotten she made. Charlie leaned over. "The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp," he said, "and it counts for every single F in the whole piece, unless you write something else next to one." Nevaeh stared at the F in bar three, and at the F in bar nine, and at the F in bar eleven, each one sitting there plain and natural and wrong.

"So they're all supposed to be sharp," she said. "The signature already did it. I just didn't read what I signed." She played the phrase again, imagining the sharps into place, and the melody snapped into focus the way a photograph does. She wondered whether the version with plain Fs had been a mistake or a discovery, whether her ear had liked the wrongness, and she could not decide, so she wrote both bars out side by side and looked at them. Sahana drifted over, still holding her highlighter like a small sceptre. "You can't subsume both into one melody," she said. "Pick. Ms. Cheung hates hedging." But Nevaeh was not sure that was true. Ms. Cheung had once kept a whole class arguing about whether a composer's intentions mattered more than a performer's, and had refused to settle it, calling it a question worth more unresolved, like something out of historiography, where you could never quite separate what happened from who got to write it down.

The clock on the wall said the room was booked until eight. Nevaeh played the F-sharp version, then the natural F, then the sharp again, and noticed that the natural one made the chord under it sound bruised, which was interesting, which was maybe even better than correct. But the rule was the rule: the signature said sharp, every F, everywhere, unless she wrote an accidental beside one to say otherwise. So the choice was real, and it was hers. She pencilled a small natural sign in front of bar three's F and felt inordinately pleased with herself, a tiny act of legislation in her own sixteen bars.

Sahana, who had been intransigent about her own piece all week, refusing every suggestion, suddenly slid her staff paper across the table. "Play mine," she said. "I want to hear it before Friday and I don't trust my own hands." Nevaeh set Sahana's page on the music stand. Sahana had chosen G major too, one sharp at the front, and there in her sixth bar was a naked F, then another in bar twelve, and Nevaeh felt the knowledge sit in her like a coin in a pocket.

"Bar six," Nevaeh said, and put her finger on it. Sahana leaned in, and the window went dark behind them, and the good keyboard waited.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
Grace had taped her poster to the folding table an hour before judging began, and now she could not stop finding faults with it. The diagram of two parallel charged plates looked crooked. Her handwritten equation for the field between them, E equals V over d, looked crooked too, and the numbers underneath looked suddenly suspect, as though the whole thing might collapse under a judge's first question.

Her project was small on purpose. Most of the gymnasium was taken up by compost reactors and solar ovens and a hovercraft built by a boy from the vocational school, but Grace had decided, against her father's advice, to do the problem nobody wanted: a plain computation of the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates. Twelve volts across plates three centimeters apart. Four hundred volts per meter. She had checked it eleven times and still checked it again, moving her pen along the arithmetic while a generator droned somewhere behind the baking-soda volcanoes.

"You should smile more," said Ellie, who had come around the table with a clipboard and the lanyard of a volunteer. "Judges are human. Humans are shallow." Ellie wanted, more than anything, to be trusted with responsibility, and had volunteered for setup, teardown, and the water station in between. She was also, Grace knew, angling to be mentioned in the local paper's photo caption, which she pretended was a joke and was not.

"That's semantics," Grace said. "Smiling more and looking honest are different things."

"They're the same thing if you're the one looking." Ellie shrugged and moved on toward the water station, and Grace smoothed the corner of the poster flat.

Mr. Khoury, who taught physics two towns over and judged every year in the same gray cardigan, arrived at ten. He did not look at the decorations, which stung, and did not look away from the numbers, which helped. He asked her to walk him through the field at the midpoint. She did, her voice steadier than she expected, and he nodded once. Then he leaned in.

"And if I put a charged dust particle there," he said, "what's the force on it?"

Grace's mind went briefly and completely white. This was not on her poster. She had computed the field and stopped, as if the field were the end of the story rather than the beginning of one. Then, out loud, slowly, she exhumed a half-remembered line from a chapter she had skimmed: "Force equals the charge times the field strength. F equals qE. So if the particle carries a charge of two nanocoulombs, the force is..." She worked it on the back of her handout. "Eight times ten to the minus seven newtons."

"And if the charge doubles?"

"Then the force doubles." It came out before she had thought it, and then she checked it and it held. The charge times the field. Twice the charge, twice the push. She looked up, almost embarrassed by how good the small certainty felt.

Mr. Khoury wrote something on his card. "You stopped your project where most students start theirs," he said. "That's either laziness or restraint." He moved on to the hovercraft, and Grace sat down on the folding chair and felt her ears burning. She had spent weeks being sanguine about her chances, telling her father that a clean calculation would speak for itself, and now she understood that the calculation had only spoken once it was used, once something rested on it, even a dust particle.

Ellie reappeared with two paper cups of water and the day's first real crisis: the judges' table had run out of judging sheets, and the head organizer had asked her, personally, to print more from the office. "He asked me," she said. "Specifically me." Grace said that was genuinely great, and found she meant it. Then she asked Ellie to hold the poster flat while she peeled off the decorative border she had spent a Saturday on, the glossy lightning bolts she now saw as a costume over the actual work. Underneath, the crooked diagram looked suddenly fine. Crooked, but hers.

When the awards were announced, Grace took third in physical sciences, behind the hovercraft and a water-filtration column that had, admittedly, actually filtered water. Ellie's name did appear in the paper, in the caption, half out of frame behind a volcano. That evening Grace cleared her desk at home, took out a fresh notebook, and wrote at the top of the first page: What else does the field touch? Below it she drew two plates, a point between them, and a small charged particle pushing off toward one side.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Natalie had wanted the job at Lakeside Day Camp since she was nine, when the counselors seemed to her the most enviable people alive, tan and loud and free to jump in the lake at will. Now she was one of them, or nearly, hired at the front desk to check kids in each morning, file the medical forms, and titrate the walkie-talkie chatter from the waterfront into short reports for Ms. Desir, who ran the camp from a folding table under a canopy. The pay was ten dollars an hour. Natalie had not negotiated, because she hadn't known negotiating was a thing eighteen-year-olds did.

The first paycheck came on a Friday in mid-July, and Arianne, who was staying the week at her aunt's place across the state line and had taken a day camp job there herself, spread both stubs out on the picnic table like cards. "Look at this," Arianne said. "You got more per hour than me. Same job, basically. I'm watching eight-year-olds in a field hockey camp."

Natalie looked. Nine dollars and something, Arianne's rate, against her own ten. "That's not much of a difference," she said, though she could see it mattered to Arianne, whose aunt charged her rent for the room, jokingly, maybe.

"It's the principle of it." Arianne flicked her stub with a finger. "We're in the next state. One highway over. How does an hour of my life cost less than an hour of yours?"

That evening, while the last parents' cars trailed dust up the gravel road, Natalie sat on the porch of the camp office with her phone and looked it up, partly for Arianne and partly because the question had begun to itch. She found a sentence she read twice: the federal minimum wage had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum. She said the date out loud to the empty porch. July 24, 2009. She had been four. The number had never moved in her entire conscious life, while everything around it, movie tickets, gas, her mother's groceries, had crept upward like a turgid river rising over its banks after weeks of rain.

She texted Arianne the sentence, then added: so nobody is making you earn less than 7.25, but the federal number is just a floor, and our state's floor is higher than your aunt's state's. Or maybe it was the city. She checked again, and it was the city, and she had to unsend and retype, and even then she wasn't sure she had the chain right, whether Arianne's camp was inside the city limits or out.

On Monday, Arianne arrived at pickup time with her aunt's dog on a leash and a face that suggested she had done her own reading. "So the whole country runs on a number from 2009," she said. "That's the part I can't get over. Somebody decided, and then everyone just kept deciding nothing for, what, my whole life?"

"Almost mine too," Natalie said. She had spent the weekend turning it over, the way she'd once turned over the fact that her grandmother's house had been cheaper than her mother's car. There was a version of this where the answer was simple and someone was to blame, and a version where it was just how laws worked, slow and sticky, and she could not make herself fully believe either one. What she kept coming back to was smaller and stranger: that an hour of a person could have a price set before that person could read.

Ms. Desir came out from under the canopy with the sign-out clipboard and overheard enough to raise an eyebrow. "Arguing economics on my porch," she said. "Good. Mind the gate, the Min boys are trying to sneak onto the dock again." She didn't offer an opinion on the minimum wage, which Natalie found, in an odd way, respectful, as if Ms. Desir trusted them to hold the question without resolving it.

Natalie walked to the gate. The Min brothers saw her coming and stalled at the water's edge, one foot on the dock, one on the grass, caught between desires. "Save it for swim block," she called. Behind her Arianne was folding the paycheck stub back into her pocket, and Natalie thought, not for the first time that summer, that she'd take the job again either way, at ten dollars or at seven twenty-five, and that she didn't know yet whether that made her grateful or cheap, and that she'd find out, probably, on some later Friday, when the envelope was thinner than she'd planned around. The gate latch clicked shut under her hand.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old solder, and Brody sat on an upturned milk crate with his grandfather's electric bass across his knees, trying to make his fingers obey. He had three weeks until the community center rehearsal, three weeks to stop sounding like a man dropping tools down a stairwell. The amp hummed beside the workbench where a coffee tin of screws had not moved in a decade. Everything in the garage belonged to someone who wasn't there anymore, and Brody had decided, without quite admitting it, that if he could learn the instrument he would somehow be keeping part of the old man in service.

Eliane came through the side door without knocking, the way she always did, carrying her keyboard under one arm and a phone in her free hand. "You're still flat," she said. "The whole time. Even I can hear it and I've been playing for two months."

"I'm tuning to the fork," Brody said, and held up the small steel fork from the drawer under the bench, its tines worn to a dull shine. He struck it on his knee, let it whine against his ear, then played his open A string. The two sounds slid against each other, close but not the same, and he adjusted the peg a fraction at a time until they locked into one.

Eliane frowned at her phone. "My tuner app says your A is a hair sharp. It wants four forty exactly. The standard tuning note is A above middle C at four forty hertz, and there's some international standards thing that fixed it. Sonia told me. She reads about this stuff." She turned the screen toward him so he could see the needle trembling at zero. "Maybe your fork is off."

He wanted to argue. The fork had lived in that drawer since before he was born, and his grandfather had been a man who measured twice and cut once, who would have said, in that dry way of his, that a phone was no substitute for steel. Brody had been half in love with that certainty all summer, the idea that the old ways were truer. But the needle was the needle, and when he struck the fork again and held the phone close, the app read the fork a few cents flat. Old steel, tired steel, or an app calibrated in some factory he'd never see. He had no way of knowing which, and that bothered him more than the smallness of the difference.

Sonia arrived the next evening with her trumpet case and her certainty about everything. "It's formalized in ISO 16," she said, when they told her. "That's the number. The whole world tunes to that A so orchestras in Tokyo and garages in this one can play together." She said it lightly, the way she said most things, but Brody heard the weight underneath: a plebiscite of sorts, millions of musicians voting with their instruments for a single pitch, and his grandfather's fork casting its lone dissent.

He thought of a night two summers ago, before the diagnosis, when his grandfather had sat on this same crate tuning an old radio by ear, twisting the dial a hair at a time while a staticky orchestra swam into focus. "Everybody wants it easy now," the old man had said, tapping the radio's wooden side. "Push a button, get an answer." Brody, fourteen and disaffected from nearly everything, had shrugged, and his grandfather had laughed at the shrug, which somehow made it all right between them. It was the last conversation they'd had that felt like a whole one.

"I keep thinking I have to pick," Brody said now, resting the bass flat across his lap. "The fork or the app. Like it's a loyalty thing." Eliane was noodling a chord line on her keyboard, half listening. Sonia oiled a valve. "But the fork is just a tool," Sonia said, not looking up. "So is the app. The note's the note either way."

He turned that over while he retuned, and it seemed to him that both things could be true at once, that a standard could be real and useful while the fork could still carry something the phone didn't, and that neither one required him to valorize it beyond what it did. The fork was a keepsake. The app was a reference. The A was the A. He tightened the string, struck the fork one last time for the sound of it alone, then set it gently back in the drawer.

The day of the rehearsal, Ms. Demir stood at the front of the community center room with a tuner app glowing on the music stand and said, "Give me an A, everyone." Trumpets, keyboards, a cello, and Brody's bass all bent toward the same small frequency, wobbling and then agreeing. He thought of the drawer, the steel, the dial on the old radio. When his turn came for the walking line in the second song, he played it clean, mostly, and Ms. Demir nodded once without stopping the band. Eliane caught his eye across the room and grinned.

Afterward, in the emptying parking lot, Sonia asked, "You bringing the fork Thursday?" and Brody said, "Always," and patted the pocket of his jacket where it lay.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
Maika spread the textbook across the picnic table, weighting one corner with a rock because the backyard wind kept lifting the page like it wanted to read ahead. Keisha sat across from her with the practice questions, and Karis lay on the grass with the graph, a printout of carbon dioxide across the last century, holding it above her face as if the rising line might fall on her.

"Question four," Keisha read. "Explain how greenhouse gases trap heat, and interpret the graph."

"I know the graph part." Maika traced the curve without touching it. "It goes up. It wiggles every year, sawtooth, but the trend is up. That part I could do in my sleep."

"Then do the other part."

"The other part is the problem." She flipped pages. The afternoon heat sat on the yard like a lid, and the drone of a neighbor's mower somewhere three streets over was making somnolence a real danger. She sat up straighter. "Okay. Greenhouse gases trap heat. The sun's radiation comes in, the Earth warms up, and the Earth sends radiation back out, and the gases in the air catch some of it on the way out. Like a blanket. Right?"

"Keep going."

"So the gases that make up most of the air do most of it." She wrote it down, transcribing her own logic into her notes as if writing it made it settled. "Nitrogen and oxygen. Ninety-nine percent of dry air, right there in the chapter. That's the trapping."

Karis lowered the graph and looked at her over the edge of the paper. "Read that bit again."

"Ninety-nine percent of dry air. It's a bold number, you have to admit."

"Read the sentence after it."

"There is no sentence after it. There's a diagram of a molecule." Maika turned the book around. Two circles, identical, joined. Then another two circles, identical, joined. Then a bent, mismatched three-circle thing. "Nitrogen. Oxygen. And that one's, I don't know, the weird one."

Karis got up, crossed the grass, and put her finger under a line of small print Maika had skimmed past twice. Maika read it, then read it again, and felt the small specific vertigo of having been confident in the wrong direction.

"No," she said.

"Yep."

"Nitrogen and oxygen make up about ninety-nine percent of dry air but they are not greenhouse gases." She said it slowly, checking each phrase against the page. "Because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation."

"So your blanket is full of holes," Keisha said. "Ninety-nine percent of it is holes."

"That can't be right. That's backwards. The most common stuff does the least?"

"Two identical atoms," Karis said. "That's the phrase. That's the whole thing."

Maika sat with it. The rock on the page, the mower still going, the wicker chair by the fence that the previous owners had left, vestigial now, its cushions long rotted and replaced with a folded tarp. She looked at the diagram again. The mismatched, bent molecule. Whatever that one was, it was the one that mattered, and it was nowhere near ninety-nine percent of anything.

"So the graph," she said. "The line going up. It's not going up because there's more air. There's always been air. It's going up because the small stuff, the trace stuff, is changing." She pulled the graph from Karis and set it beside the diagram, side by side on the table, and put the rock on both. "The trapping is done by the rare gases, and we're adding more of them, so more outgoing radiation gets caught, so it climbs."

"Question four," Keisha said, tapping the page. "Answer it out loud. Full answer."

Maika gave it: the radiation in, the radiation out, the absorption by the molecules that were not nitrogen and oxygen, the two-identical-atoms problem, the sawtooth wiggles on the graph that she guessed were seasons, though the book did not say, and the century-long climb that the book did say. Keisha marked her pauses with a pencil, tallying them like fouls.

"Seasons is a guess," Karis said. "You said guess."

"I said guess. I'm keeping the guess and I'm labeling it." Maika wrote it in the margin, small, with a question mark. "The wiggles might be seasons. Uncertain. That's honest."

"Ms. Wijaya would give you half credit for that."

"Ms. Wijaya would give me half credit for the whole thing, honestly, if I stop there. There's a part two to question four." Maika turned the page. "'If the atmosphere were entirely nitrogen and oxygen, what would happen to the graph?'"

The three of them went quiet. The mower stopped somewhere, and the yard was just wind and the page straining under the rock.

"There wouldn't be a graph," Karis said finally. "Nothing to measure climbing."

"Nothing climbing," Maika said, and wrote it down.

Keisha looked at her watch, then at the sky, then at the two of them. "Quiz each other," she said, standing. "I'm getting the flashcards."

She went inside through the screen door, and it clapped shut behind her, and Maika flipped the book back to the diagram of the two identical circles and the one bent stranger, and put her finger on the stranger.

"You," she said.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
The bus shelter outside Marlowe's Diner smelled like fryer grease and rain, and Angelina read the help wanted sign through the window for the fourth time before she went in. Memphis had made her promise to stop stalling. "It's a diner," Memphis had said on the walk over, "not a courtroom. The worst they can do is say no and give you a free glass of water."

That was before Memphis found out about the interview part. There was no application form at Marlowe's, just a conversation with the manager on Saturday afternoon, which meant Angelina had four days to figure out how to talk about herself like a person who deserved a paycheck. Four days was a long time to cogitate, and she had used most of it badly, lying on her bedroom floor composing answers that all sounded like they belonged to somebody else.

It was Memphis who came to the rescue on Thursday night, arriving at Angelina's window seat with a printed page from some career website. "My cousin says this is how you answer interview questions," Memphis said, tapping the paper. "It's called the STAR method." Angelina read the page twice. The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result. "So it's a way of telling a story," Memphis said. "Situation, task, action, result. Like a recipe."

"It sounds like chicanery," Angelina said. "Like a trick for making normal people sound impressive." Memphis shrugged, unbothered, phlegmatic in the way that made teachers think Memphis didn't care about anything, which was exactly wrong. "It's not a trick if the story's true," Memphis said. "It's just a shape. Pick something that actually happened and pour it in."

The problem was that everything that actually happened felt too small. Then Angelina remembered the group project from last spring, the one where Cody had vanished for two weeks and the other two members had quietly decided the whole thing would collapse, and Angelina had stayed up until one in the morning rebuilding a presentation she hadn't broken. She practiced telling it in the shower, in the kitchen while her mother stirred soup, and once, disastrously, out loud in chemistry until Cody leaned over and asked if she was having a crisis. Cody was the missing person in the story, which made practicing it in front of Cody a special kind of awkward, but Cody only said, "Just don't make me the villain. Make me, like, a scheduling conflict."

Saturday came cold and bright. The restaurant was half empty at three in the afternoon, booths wiped down, a radio somewhere playing old soul. The manager was a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, and he slid into the booth across from her with a coffee he clearly didn't intend to finish. He asked the usual things, why she wanted the job, whether she could work weekends, and then he leaned back and said, "Tell me about a time things went wrong and you had to fix them."

The question hung there. Angelina felt the shape of it before she could name it, and then the shape had a name: situation, task, action, result. She started with the situation, the four-person project and the two vanished weeks, and she kept Cody vague the way she'd promised. The task had been the presentation, due in five days with half the slides missing. The action, hers alone: she called a meeting nobody wanted, divided what was left into pieces small enough that no one could claim they were too busy, and rebuilt the opening section herself. The result, when she got to it, surprised her, because she had never actually said it out loud before: they got a B plus, the group still spoke to each other, and Cody thanked her after class, quietly, like an apology.

The manager was quiet for a moment, tapping his cup. "Most kids your age tell me they're a hard worker and a fast learner," he said. "You told me a story I can picture." He asked about Saturdays again, and about whether she could carry a tray, and then he stood and shook her hand and said the aprons were in the back and could she start next weekend.

Walking out, Angelina turned the whole thing over. The STAR method had not made her someone else; it had only given her a frame to hold a true thing in, which felt less like a trick and more like learning that a true thing, told with a shape, lands harder. She was still not certain she could carry a tray, or that the job wouldn't grind her down by October, or that a B plus was anything to build a story on. But Memphis was waiting at the bus shelter with two phone screens glowing and a grin already forming.

"Well?" Memphis said.

"I start Saturday," Angelina said. "Now teach me to carry a tray."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Guessing a whole number from 1 to 100 by always picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses, which is binary search in game form.
story:
The buzzer went at four minutes remaining, and Aaron's screen still showed the fault. Their robot had to locate a block on the sorted shelf array, grab it, and deliver it before the clock, and every run the arm swept left to right, checking each slot in turn, until it ran out of time two slots short of the target.

"Run it again," Brenden said, hovering.

"Running it again won't change the math." Aaron pulled up the log. Sixty-four slots. The arm read them one at a time. Worst case, sixty-four reads. He said this out loud and Colin, across the pit table, made a small defeated noise and began transcribing their times onto the score sheet, as though documenting a loss would make it official.

The fault was in his code, and his code alone. He'd written the search himself, back when the array was sixteen slots and nobody cared. Then the new shelf arrived, and Ms. Dlamini, walking the aisles of the pit area, had stopped at their table an hour ago and looked at the sweep of the arm and said only, "You know your data's sorted," and moved on. She hadn't said anything else. She never did. Aaron had spent the intervening hour resenting her for it.

He stared at the array in his editor, indices marching down the page, and something surfaced, a summer kitchen, his grandfather's virulent opinions about neighbors' lawns and, between rants, a game. Pick a number from one to a hundred, his grandfather had said, sliding a cookie across the table. Higher or lower, I'll tell you. His grandfather guessed by feel and lost constantly, and one afternoon, out of pure impatience, Aaron had stopped guessing numbers he liked and started guessing fifty. Then, depending on the answer, the middle of whatever range was left. Twenty-five or seventy-five. Then again. He remembered counting: never more than seven guesses, not once, and his grandfather refusing to play anymore by the third day, calling it unnatural.

He had never thought about it again. It had just been a way to win cookies. But the array on his screen was sorted, the way the number line had been sorted, and a number line and a sorted array were, in the only way that mattered here, the same thing. Sixty-four slots, and if he checked the middle slot first, he'd know which half the target was in, and he could throw the other half away entirely.

"That's binary search," Colin said, looking over his shoulder at what Aaron was typing. "My cousin wouldn't shut up about it. Halving the range every guess." Colin said it flatly, the way he reported anything he knew, and went back to the score sheet.

"Two ten," Brenden called, watching the queue monitor. Two minutes, ten seconds.

Aaron deleted the sweep loop. He wrote low and high, a middle, the comparison, the halving. Sixty-four became thirty-two became sixteen. His hands were doing it faster than his certainty about it; somewhere underneath, he still half believed the arm needed to see every slot, that skipping was cheating, the way his grandfather had seemed to feel it was. He checked the comparison twice, changed one sign, and uploaded.

"Can we test it first?" Brenden asked.

"No time." Aaron pressed run.

The arm read slot thirty-two, adjusted, read slot forty-eight, adjusted. On the sixth read it closed on the target and carried it across the field. The clock showed fifty-one seconds left. Brenden grabbed his shoulder and shook it and Colin stood up so fast his chair rolled into the pit table behind them.

They got called to the field. Ms. Dlamini was at the scorer's table and watched their run without expression, and their robot found its block and delivered it with thirty-eight seconds to spare. Afterward she came by their table, glanced at the monitor, at the middle-first loop still on screen, and said, "Better," and moved on toward the next pit.

Brenden was already arguing that they should halve everything from now on, that maybe the drive code too, the vision, all of it, and Aaron was nodding while not quite agreeing in his head. It had worked because the array was sorted. He understood that much, and he understood the seven guesses from the summer, though he couldn't have said why seven exactly, only that it had always been enough at the kitchen table and it was enough here. Whether it would be enough if the array changed size, whether it still worked if something in the middle got moved, he wrote on the back of Colin's score sheet to test later, and underlined twice.

"Queue's closing," the volunteer called.

Aaron closed the laptop and said, "Pass me the battery."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The house smelled of cardamom and old paper, as it always did, and Michael carried his copy of Jane Eyre to the kitchen table where his grandmother was slicing oranges into thin, even wheels. He had come here because the apartment he shared with his mother was too loud for studying, and his grandmother never asked why he needed quiet. She only slid a plate toward him and said the porch was dry now if he wanted it.

He was supposed to write about Jane's choice to leave Rochester, using a critical lens, and the assignment sheet in his folder listed options like items on a menu. Feminist. Marxist. Postcolonial. He had chosen feminist because Xavier had chosen Marxist, and Xavier always claimed his lens first, like a seat on a bus.

Xavier arrived at four with Ahmed, both of them damp from the walk. They settled on the porch cushions, Ahmed tucking a blanket around Xavier's legs without being asked, because Xavier ran cold even in September. Ahmed was there for moral support and free oranges; he hadn't read the book. "Summarize it fast," he said, reaching for the plate.

"Plain governess, rich brooding man with a mad wife hidden in the attic," Michael said. "She loves him, finds out about the wife, and leaves. Then she comes back after his wife dies and the house burns down and he's blind, and marries him."

"Okay, so what's the debate?"

Xavier flipped his notebook open. "The debate is whether she's free. The Marxist says she leaves because she has nothing, no property, no family, and comes back only when she has inherited money and he's dependent on her. That's material conditions shaping the whole plot."

"And the feminist says?"

Michael had a page of notes he wasn't sure about. He remembered Mr. Russo, last spring, standing at the whiteboard while a kid argued that Catherine in Wuthering Heights was just dramatic. Mr. Russo hadn't corrected him. He'd asked, quietly, whether anyone had ever wanted something so exactly matched to what the world wanted them to want that they couldn't tell the difference. The class had gone silent, and Michael had written the question down without knowing why. He found it now, folded between two pages of Jane Eyre.

"Here's the problem," Michael said. "Jane says she chooses. She says it constantly. Reader, she tells us, I married him. But how do we know a choice is yours? What if what you want was trained into you?"

Ahmed ate another orange slice. "Then nobody's free ever, which seems like a cheat."

"That's what I thought too," Michael said. Then he'd found his grandmother's shelf. He got up, went inside, and came back with a thick grey book, its spine cracked white at one place. "My grandmother has this. Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, published in 1949. There's a line in it." He found the page by feel. "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman."

"Meaning what?" Ahmed asked.

"Meaning society shapes it. Womanhood is built, not inborn." Michael set the book down between them. "So the lens isn't Jane lied about choosing. It's that wanting isn't a pure place you can stand on. Jane was raised to be modest, poor, grateful, self-erasing. She wants Rochester, sure. She also wants to be good, and her idea of good came from somewhere."

Xavier frowned at the book. "That could extenuate anything, though. Every terrible husband in literature gets a pass because his society made him."

"That's the trap," Michael admitted. "It's not an excuse machine. Beauvoir isn't saying nobody's responsible. She's saying you have to look at the training before you can judge the choice." He paused. "Or I think that's what she's saying. I might be overreading it."

"Overreading is the assignment," Xavier said, and Ahmed laughed.

His grandmother came out with tea, four cups, and set the strongest one in front of Xavier because she had noticed he was the one shivering. She looked at the grey book on the table and touched its cover briefly, the way you touch a dog you know. "I read that when I was not much older than you," she said. "It was quieter then, what it said. Everything was quiescent, and this book was not." She didn't stay to explain. She went back to her oranges.

They worked until the light went orange itself. Xavier drafted a Marxist paragraph with real momentum; Michael's feminist paragraph kept circling. He wrote that Jane's choices were real within her limits, that leaving was possibly the one act her training couldn't account for, since a good poor governess was supposed to stay and suffer quietly. Then he crossed out "possibly" and put it back in.

"You're doing the both-things thing," Ahmed said, watching him.

"I'm doing the honest thing," Michael said. "I don't know if Jane is free or just better at disguising the cage. I know she walks out that door in the morning with no money and no plan, and that's not what a trained woman does." He closed his notebook. "Maybe that's the essay. What stays uncertain."

Xavier raised his teacup. "To the trained woman who walked anyway."

"To the trained woman who walked anyway," Ahmed echoed, and clinked his cup so hard against the others that tea sloshed onto the blanket, and Michael went inside for a towel.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The pit smelled like solder and energy drinks, and Juliette's laptop had chosen this exact moment to die. She pressed the power button three times, the way you cajole a stubborn machine, then once more with feeling, and the screen finally flickered back to her half-written code just as Emy leaned over her shoulder.

"Is that why the arm motor isn't responding?" Emy asked. "Because your arm class is a haunted house?"

Juliette turned the laptop so Emy could see the whole mess. She had been trying to write a Java class for the arm, with the joint angles and the grip strength kept private, only reachable through getter methods, the way Ms. Berg had drilled into them until it felt like a law of nature. Somewhere in there she had also written a test, a small program whose only job was to prove the class worked, and the test kept failing in a way she couldn't read.

"Mr. Gosling is punishing me," she said.

"Who?" Emy squinted at the screen.

"James Gosling. He designed Java." Juliette gestured at the error like it was his personal handwriting. "I read it last night instead of debugging, which tells you something about my priorities."

Ewan slid into the third chair with a paper plate of nachos balanced on his knee. "Java's from the nineties, right? My dad says it like it's ancient."

"Nineteen ninety-five," Juliette said. "Sun Microsystems put it out then. So it's older than all of us, which is honestly rude of it."

"Older than us and still making you cry," Ewan said, and stole one of her nachos as tax.

The queue for their next match was twenty minutes out, so she bent back into the code. The arm class held its fields private, and every other part of the program had to knock politely and ask through the getters. She liked the theory of it, the idea of a polite boundary between the arm's business and everyone else's. What she hadn't liked, until this weekend, was testing. Tests had always struck her as extrinsic, something done to code from the outside for a grade, a sticker on a drawing. Now, with a referee whistle going off somewhere behind her, the test was the only thing standing between her team and an arm that flopped like a dead fish in front of three hundred people.

She built a small test object, set the grip strength to a number, and asked the class to hand it back through the getter. The number that came out was wrong. Not garbage, which would have been almost comforting, but wrong in a quiet, plausible way, like a witness who had rehearsed.

"There," Emy said, pointing. "You're setting it twice. Look."

She was. Juliette had a second assignment buried below the first, a leftover from an earlier attempt, and the second write was clobbering the first. She deleted it, ran the test again, and watched the expected number and the actual number finally agree, sitting side by side like twins on a bus.

"Oh," she said, and then, with more dignity than she felt, "I knew that."

"You absolutely did not," said Ewan, but he said it while writing her name on the whiteboard under the heading "Todays Heroes," next to a drawing of a fish.

While they waited for the match, Ms. Berg wandered over with a coffee and asked, in her mild way, what they'd learned. Juliette started to say something about syntax, then stopped. What she had actually learned was stranger. At school, code was a thing you finished and handed in; here, code was a thing you argued with until one of you blinked. Both were true, she supposed, and she wasn't yet sure which one she'd believe in September.

"It's like genus and species," she said instead. "The class is the general kind of thing, and each test drags it down to the specific, to what's actually true."

Ms. Berg raised an eyebrow. "That's a Latin way to talk about a compiler error."

"There was a compiler error," Juliette said, "and I have triumphed over it."

Their match was called. The robot rolled out onto the field with its arm class held private and tidy inside it, getters like little doors with proper hinges. Juliette stood at the driver station with her fingers over the controls, and when the arm rose on cue and closed its grip around the first ring, she heard Emy scream her name from the stands, and she screamed back.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store still had its lines, faded white stripes that made the whole asphalt plain feel like graph paper nobody had filled in. Sophie sat in the driver's seat of Ms. Walker's hatchback with her hands at ten and two, the way she had practiced on a bus seat for weeks, and waited to be told what to do. Ms. Walker, who taught sophomore English and had offered to give Sophie her first lesson before college started, set down a fistful of orange cones on the far side of the lot and walked back slowly, counting her paces.

"Here's the game," Ms. Walker said, settling into the passenger seat. "We're going to find your braking distance at twenty miles an hour. You drive straight at those cones, brake as hard as you can when I say now, and we'll see where you stop. Then we double the speed and do it again. But first, guess. Twenty to forty. How much longer to stop?"

Sophie thought of her mother, who drove as though braking were a moral failing, and of her physics teacher, who had liked to say that intuition was a liar with a kind face. She tried to introspect, to look honestly at what she actually believed rather than what she wanted to believe, and found the answer embarrassingly simple. "Twice as long," she said. "It's twice the speed, so twice the distance. That's the guess I'd defend."

"Good," Ms. Walker said, in the tone of someone who has heard a wrong answer many times before and still finds it likable. "Defend it in the car." She checked the lot, which was empty except for a torpid pigeon by the loading dock that did not bother to lift its head even when the engine turned over. "First gear, feet off both pedals until I say now."

The car inched forward, then found its pace. Sophie had imagined driving would feel like the moment in a pool when your feet leave the bottom, but it felt more like carrying something breakable across a dark room. Ms. Walker said now, Sophie pressed the brake, and the car stopped a car length and a half short of the cones, close enough that she could see the gravel caught in their rubber bases.

They measured with a tape from the back of the front tire to the chalk mark Ms. Walker had dropped at the braking point. Twenty-two feet. Sophie wrote it on her palm in ballpoint because her phone was in her bag in the back seat, a decision that already felt like an old driver's habit. Then Ms. Walker had her do it again at the same speed, and the second run was twenty-one feet, and Sophie understood that even a measurement had a mood.

"Now the interesting one," Ms. Walker said. "We double it. Forty miles an hour." She looked at Sophie over the rims of her sunglasses. "Walk your cones out first. Where do you think you'll stop?"

Sophie stood in the middle of the lot with the tape dragging behind her and tried to hold two ideas at once. Her mother would say twice, no question, the way she said everything, quickly and finally. Her physics teacher would say nothing at all and wait, because he believed answers you were handed were answers you never kept. Somewhere between them, Sophie laid the tape out to forty-four feet, marked it, then stood there a long moment, sweating in the August heat, before she picked the chalk back up and walked the tape out again, to eighty-eight.

"That's a lot of room," Ms. Walker said, watching her.

"If I'm wrong, we'll know," Sophie said. "That's the whole point of the cones."

The run at forty felt different in her hands, the steering wheel suddenly an animal with opinions, and when Ms. Walker said now, the brake held her foot back, resisting, and the lot kept coming, the cones swelling, the pigeon at the loading dock finally lifting itself away with an offended flap. The car stopped. Sophie put it in park, and neither of them said anything while she walked the tape from her front tire to the chalk mark. Eighty-six feet. Four times twenty-two, give or take the mood of the measurement.

"Twice as fast," she said out loud, to the cones or to her mother or to the version of herself that had defended the wrong answer an hour ago. "Four times as long to stop." She looked down the whole empty length of the lot, imagining it filled with taillights and rain, and then she rolled up the tape and got back in the car.

"Same speed again," she said, hands at ten and two. "I want to feel it when it's small, before I have to trust it when it isn't."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
story:
Luke had done the math, and the math said the car was his. He told his father this in the parking lot of the dealership, twice, in case the first telling hadn't landed. Nine thousand dollars for the silver hatchback, two thousand from his summer mowing money, seven thousand borrowed, gone in a year if he worked weekends at the garden center. His father said nothing, which Luke took, generously, as agreement.

Inside, a salesman in a gray vest whose name tag Luke never read led them to a desk shaped like a wing. The hatchback sat in the showroom under the lights, and Luke liked to believe it was the same one he had seen online, though the listing had been for a blue one. Numbers bloomed across a printed sheet: seventy-two months, an interest rate, a monthly payment circled in red pen. Luke read the payment and then the total at the bottom, and the two figures refused to be friends. The total was bigger. Much bigger. He asked why, and the salesman smiled the way adults smile when they've been waiting all day for someone to ask.

"Interest," the salesman said. "You're not just paying back seven thousand. You're paying for borrowing it. Every month, they charge you a percentage of what you still owe." He tapped the total. Luke stared at it and felt something in him, some vestigial certainty from the parking lot, go quiet. His father, who had said nothing, now said, "Keep reading."

They did not buy the car that afternoon. In the lot, his father's old truck waiting in the sun, Luke sat on a concrete bumper and texted Elianna, who worked afternoons at the credit union on Marsh Road and who had once explained the whole school grading system to him in one text thread. She texted back within a minute, which Luke interpreted as devotion, though Addison later pointed out she answered everyone that fast. He asked about savings accounts, because a thought had surfaced, small and sharp: if interest made borrowed money cost more over time, what did it do to saved money?

Elianna didn't answer by text. She said come by after five, so he did. The credit union smelled like carpet cleaner, and she slid two brochures across the counter when the lobby emptied, one for each of their savings accounts. "Same rate," she said. "Different compounding. This one's monthly, this one's yearly." She wrote the formula on the back of a deposit slip in blue pen, quick, like it cost her nothing: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). She tapped the n. "n is how many times per year interest is added." The account that compounded monthly came out slightly larger, she said, showed him the two endings on the calculator, and the difference was small, almost insultingly small, but real, and it pointed one direction only.

Luke wanted to say he had known this already. He said, "Right, obviously," and Elianna looked at him with one eyebrow until he admitted he hadn't, and she laughed, and it didn't feel like losing. What he understood, standing there, was that he had spent a year believing money was a flat thing, a number that moved in straight lines, and it wasn't. It curved. Borrow seven thousand and the curve bent against you; put two thousand away at sixteen and it bent for you, slowly, quietly, more the longer you left it alone. He thought of determinism, which they'd argued about in seminar, the idea that everything was already decided. Maybe money was like that, he thought, the formula deciding everything in advance. But then Elianna said, "It only works if you don't touch it," and that part was on him. The curve didn't choose. He did.

He told Addison about it later at the gas station where they bought slushies, and Addison, who was saving for nothing and proud of it, said a year of interest on two thousand wouldn't buy a tire. "A slightly bigger number is still small," Addison said, and Luke couldn't argue, because it was true and it wasn't, the way things managed to be both. He didn't have the hatchback. He had a job interview at the garden center on Thursday and a deposit slip in his pocket with the formula on it, blue ink going soft at the folds.

At home his father asked, over dinner, whether he was still thinking about the car. Luke started to say yes and stopped. He said he was thinking about being nineteen, which made his father set down his fork, and what three years of a savings account looked like, whatever it came to exactly. He hadn't run the numbers on that part yet. He put the deposit slip on the table between them, the crease facing up, and his father pulled it closer to the lamp and read it slowly, twice.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
Laura had claimed the garage as her study three weeks ago, dragging out the broken lawnmower and her mother's boxes of canning jars, and now the card table by the window held her chemistry textbook, a mug of cold tea, and Mr. Wang's old chemistry set, which he had lent her the day she told him she wanted to understand equilibrium before the unit test.

He had said almost nothing when he handed it over. "The bottles are labelled. The book will tell you more than I would." That was the kind of teacher he was, and it annoyed her and then it didn't, because she was starting to see what he was doing.
