The problem she could not put down came from Aya, who had leaned across the aisle in class that morning and said, "Okay, so if cooling an exothermic reaction gives you more product, why would any factory run it hot on purpose? That's like choosing the worse option. Mr. Wang wouldn't answer, he just smiled and said to think about it, which means he wants us to hurt a little first."

Aya was coming over, and so was Maxx, whose older cousin worked at a chemical plant two towns over and who had promised, with the confidence of someone repeating something half-heard at a barbecue, that "they run ammonia reactors at like four or five hundred degrees, basically as hot as a pizza oven, and the yield is worse, and nobody cares." Laura had written this in her notebook and then underlined it twice, because if it was true, then the textbook was leaving something out, and she wanted to know what.

They sat on overturned milk crates around the card table, and Maxx read the cousin's text messages aloud while Aya drew the reaction on the garage's chalky concrete floor with a piece of sidewalk chalk: nitrogen plus hydrogen going to ammonia, arrows in both directions, the word exothermic in a box. "So Le Chatelier," Aya said. "The system pushes back against whatever you do to it. Heat it, and it shifts to consume the heat, which means less ammonia. Cool it, and it shifts toward ammonia."

"Which says run it cold," Laura said. "All day, run it cold. And your cousin says they run it hot." She said the sentence again in her head and felt the two ideas refusing to suture together, the way two pieces of fabric will not join unless someone chooses to stitch them, and the stitch was the thing she was missing.

Then it came to her the way small things do, sideways, while she was staring at the chalk arrows. The arrows pointed both ways. Reactions sitting at equilibrium were still doing nothing, in a sense, still balancing. "Wait," she said. "We keep talking about how much ammonia you get if you wait forever. What if cold is only better if you can wait forever?"

Maxx frowned at his phone. "My cousin says the lines run all day, they don't wait for anything."

"Exactly," Laura said. "So how fast does it actually go when it's cold? Mr. Wang said the word once and I wrote it down. Rate." She flipped to the back pages of her notebook. "If the reaction is too slow when it's cold, then a plant could sit there getting a beautiful percentage of ammonia out of a mixture that barely changes all week. Hotter gives you less ammonia at equilibrium, but the reaction actually moves." She looked up. "So they're not choosing the worse option. They're choosing a different question. How much per hour instead of how much eventually."

Aya was quiet for a moment, chalk dust on her fingers. "So which is right?"

"That's a tautological question," Laura said, and then laughed at herself, because it was the kind of thing Mr. Wang said. "Sorry. I mean, right for what. Right depends on what you're optimizing. The textbook is right about equilibrium. The plant is right about rate. Both, and they disagree about the temperature." She tapped the chalk arrows on the floor. "I still don't know the number where you'd switch, or whether there even is one number, and I don't know how they pick it. Maybe that's next year's question."

Maxx texted his cousin and read the reply aloud: "He says there's a whole cooling loop after the reactor and they recycle the unreacted gas back through, which honestly just raises more questions."

"Everything raises more questions," Aya said. "That's the whole subject."

Laura poured the cold tea out into the flowerbed by the garage door and went back inside for the kettle. "Then let's do the one where we change the temperature," she said, unstoppering the first bottle.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A first-person narrator can report only what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say, while a third-person omniscient narrator can reveal any character's thoughts.
story:
Julia spread the two books on the table by the window, the novel for Mr. Joseph's class and her own copy, already flagged with torn paper scraps at every scene where the narrator lied. Across from her, Victor was supposed to be drafting the essay due Friday. Instead he had his chin in his hand, watching her.

"Page forty," she said. "She says she went home right after the party. But page sixty, she mentions the colour of Arianne's car at midnight. She wasn't home. She was in the car."

"So she's a liar. Write that. Three paragraphs, done."

It wasn't done, though, and that was the problem. Julia had spent a week proving the narrator lied, and Mr. Joseph had written in the margin of her draft: You have shown what she hides. Now show me what the point of view hides. She'd read the sentence eleven times on the bus and still didn't know what it asked.

Arianne arrived with her bag slung forward, already talking. "The coffee machine at the place near the pool is broken, so I got it from the gas station, don't judge me." She set the cup down beside Julia's notes and peered at the open book. "Still on that narrator? She was the only interesting part. She could make you believe anything."

"That's what I keep getting wrong," Julia said. "I keep saying she makes us believe things. But she doesn't. She just tells it, and we believe it, because she's the only one telling." She turned the notebook toward Arianne. "A first-person narrator can only report what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say. There's nobody else in the room. Everything I don't know about the story, I don't know because of her."

Victor pulled his headphones down around his neck. "So what's the essay?"

"I'm going to rewrite one scene."

She chose the scene in the kitchen, the night of the party, the narrator and her mother arguing about money. In the novel it ran half a page, all the narrator's acid commentary, her mother reduced to a series of absurd remarks about an annuity the narrator considered a fantasy. Julia copied the dialogue into her notebook exactly as printed. Then, below it, she wrote the scene again, word for word, but this time she let herself move where the novel's narrator could not. She wrote what the mother was thinking as she spoke about the annuity. She wrote what the mother knew and had been carrying through the whole chapter, the notice from the bank folded in her coat pocket, the diurnal dread of opening the mailbox each morning. The mother's thoughts, which the printed page had never once shown, filled the margin in Julia's small cramped hand.

"There," Victor said, reading over her arm. "That's a different story."

"It's the same story," Julia said. But her voice came out uncertain, and she heard it. She read the two versions again. In the first, the mother was a fool. In the second, the mother was a woman protecting her daughter from a fact, and the narrator, who could only tell what she saw and chose to say, had seen the protection and mistaken it for stupidity. The reader trusted the narrator because there was no one to correct her. A narrator who could move into any character's mind could have shown the folded notice in one line.

"So the point of view isn't just style," Arianne said slowly. "It's the lock on the information."

Mr. Joseph came by on his rounds, the way he did after school, collecting abandoned paper cups with one hand. He looked at the two versions side by side, said nothing for a moment, then tapped the notebook. "Whose thoughts are these?"

"The mother's. The original narrator can't reach them. I wanted to see what she was keeping from me." Julia hesitated. "I still think the narrator is unreliable. That part of my essay was right. But I was writing like she chose to deceive us, and I don't think that's exactly it anymore. Some of it she chose. Some of it she couldn't reach, because she only has herself. I can't always tell which is which."

"That's not a weakness in the essay," Mr. Joseph said, and moved on toward the periodicals with the cup.

Arianne had taken the notebook and was reading the rewritten scene, her lips moving slightly, the gas station coffee going cold beside her. She looked up.

"Do the kitchen scene one more time," she said. "Do it from the mother's point of view, her telling it, first person, and see if she lies too."

Julia turned to a clean page.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
Emily had played "Pomp and Circumstance" so many times in the past two weeks that her fingers found the valves without her, the way a hand finds a banister in a dark house. She stood in the third row of the wind ensemble, on the far side of the folding chairs where the seniors would sit, close enough to hear the buzz of the generators and the principal testing the microphone with a soft, repeating "check, check." The football field had been transformed overnight: crepe paper on the fence, a rented stage, the goalposts wearing balloons like scarves. She was graduating today, and she was also working, because she had promised Mr. Brennan she would cover the march even though it was her own ceremony.

Two nights before, at the last rehearsal, she had finally asked the question that had been sitting in her mouth all spring. "Why this song? Every school in the country plays it. Who decided?"

Brogan, who played baritone and had known her since seventh grade, had lowered his horn. "It's Elgar," he said, as if that settled it. Klara looked up from her flute case, and Emily could see her deciding whether to answer or to let Brogan's confidence stand. Klara could not help herself. "It became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905," she said. "Elgar was there. They gave him an honorary doctorate of music." She said it quickly, almost apologizing, and then added, "My mom went to Yale, so I've heard the story about four hundred times."

Emily had turned that over while the ensemble ran the trio section again. She had expected some old law, some congressional decree, and instead it was an accident of imitation: one school borrowed it from another, and the borrowing spread until it became ritual. The word that came to her on the walk home was interpolate, from math class, the way you estimate a value between two known points. Nobody had legislated the march into graduation. Enough people had filled in the space between tradition and habit that the song simply appeared, as if it had always been there.

Now, under a sky the color of a peeled plum, the seniors began to file in. Emily watched her classmate Jaycee fix the tassel of the girl in front of her, who had been crying since the parking lot; watched Mr. Brennan leave the podium for a moment to hand a spare gown to a boy whose mother had forgotten his on the kitchen table. The band started the march. Emily's lips found the first note.

There was a flashback then, uninvited. She was nine, at her sister's graduation in this same stadium, sitting on her mother's shoulders with her sandals dangling, and when the band began the same melody she had asked, loudly, why the sad song, and her mother had said, "It's not sad, it's proud," and Emily, nine and certain, had said it could be both. Her mother had laughed and said maybe. That was the first time she understood that two things could be true at once and that adults didn't always like holding them together.

Because that was the trouble now, too. Half of her felt the ceremony was gratuitous, an hour of rented pageantry for a milestone that mostly meant moving out of her bedroom. The other half had cried last night folding her gown on the bed. And there was a third feeling, quieter, that Klara's fact had given her: the strangeness of joining a line of strangers, of inheriting a song from a composer who never imagined a girl in a rented stadium with a borrowed trumpet, her grandmother in row four taking photographs of everything, including the empty chairs. The ritual wasn't hollow or full. It was carried, hand to hand, and nobody remembered who first picked it up.

Between repetitions of the march, while the last rows filed in, Brogan leaned toward her and whispered, "If you ever write the tell-all book about why we play this, I want a cut." Klara, on his other side, said, "I'll settle for a footnote," and Emily said, "Fine, but the footnote is just me admitting I still don't know if the song chose us or we chose it." Brogan made a face at her, the same face he made when she overthought anything. "You can't know that," he said. "That's like asking who invented wearing hats." She was still deciding whether that counted as pedantry or wisdom when Mr. Brennan's cue hand came up.

She raised the trumpet. The final class of the morning was finding its seats, her own name somewhere among them in alphabetical order after the band was released, and her grandmother had stopped photographing empty chairs and was waving at her with both hands. Emily played the opening phrase straight through, and watched the principal step forward to the microphone.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
The deadline was three o'clock, because that was when Ms. Kaminski locked the activities office and the budget forms went to the school board, and Grace had until then to decide whether the Warren High Ledger would sign a deal with Kessler's Home Furnishings or ask readers for money instead.

She sat in the media studies classroom during fourth period, the form half filled out in front of her, while Ms. Kaminski took attendance in her dour way, ticking names without looking up. The Kessler deal was concrete: eight hundred dollars a year for a banner on the paper's website and a quarter page in each print issue, plus final say over any story that mentioned furniture, mattresses, or "related retail concerns." That last phrase was in the contract. Grace had read it four times.

"It's not censorship," Zachary said, leaning across the aisle. "It's a business relationship. Real papers do this all the time. Somebody owns them, and that somebody has opinions."

"That's exactly my problem," Grace said.

Hailey spun her chair around from the row in front. "Then don't take the money. Run on nothing. Very pure, very broke."

Grace pulled up the slide Ms. Kaminski had left on the projector from the first week of term, a wall of news logos sorted by owner, and she thought about how she'd felt that day, the small vertigo of realizing that the logo she'd trusted since middle school sat inside a box belonging to a company that also owned a film studio and a chain of stations. She had asked her dad about it that night, and he'd said, gently, that everything was owned by someone, and the trick was learning who. It had sounded wise at the time. Now it sounded like a heuristic, a shortcut that saved you from having to look further, and Grace was tired of shortcuts.

At lunch, in the classroom again because the library was closed, Hailey dumped her tray beside Grace's laptop and said she'd found something. "That nonprofit I mentioned. ProPublica. Look."

Grace read the page twice. Founded in 2007, funded by donations, no ads. And in 2010 it won a Pulitzer Prize, the first online news source ever to do it. She sat back. It wasn't proof of anything, exactly, but it was evidence, and evidence was more than she'd had an hour ago.

"So donations instead of ads," Hailey said. "They did it. It can instantiate the whole model, your model, the thing you keep saying we should be."

"That's not what instantiate means," Grace said, and Hailey waved her off, and Zachary arrived with the second half of the problem: he'd counted their readership, such as it was, four hundred site visits a month and a print run of three hundred, most of which ended up under lab stools. If every reader gave five dollars, they'd clear the Kessler money. If one in ten did, they couldn't afford printer paper.

"Then it's a bet," Grace said. "Not a principle. A bet on whether people value us."

"Everything's a bet," Zachary said. "Kessler's betting we're cheap."

Ms. Kaminski, who had been watering the fern by the window as though she weren't listening, said without turning, "The form still needs a signature by three." She never told them what to do. She'd told them in September that her job was to make the consequences visible, not to choose for them, and Grace had thought it was an abdication then, and thought it might be the most respectful thing an adult had ever done for her, and had never settled which.

Grace remembered being twelve, selling wrapping paper for the soccer team, and the sponsor on the order forms being the orthodontist whose son played keeper, and how she'd asked her mother whether the sponsor got something for it, and her mother had laughed and said, goodwill, sweetheart. Twelve-year-old Grace had accepted that. Sixteen-year-old Grace understood that goodwill was a purchase like any other, just with a longer receipt.

She filled in the donation box on the form and left the Kessler line blank, then set up a payments page with a goal meter, then wrote a short post explaining, in plain sentences, that the paper would rather be accountable to four hundred readers than to one furniture store, and that if the money didn't come, the paper would shrink, and that was a real risk and she was taking it anyway. Hailey proofread it. Zachary, who had argued for the ads until the last minute, clicked publish without being asked, which Grace understood to be his way of conceding.

By two forty they'd raised eleven dollars, all of it from Hailey's aunts. Ms. Kaminski collected the form at three o'clock exactly, read the top half, and said only, "Noted." That evening the meter sat at thirty-five dollars, and Grace refreshed it once, twice, then closed the laptop and went downstairs, where her dad asked how the fundraiser was going, and she said, "Ask me in April," and got herself a glass of water.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The application had been one page, and Charles had expected everything after it to be equally simple. It was not. Ms. Mercado, who owned the coffee shop on Fell Street, had hired him in under ten minutes on a Tuesday afternoon, shaking his hand over the register while the grinder behind her ran. Then she slid a clipboard across the counter and said, "Do these at the table by the window, take your time," and walked off to argue with a delivery man about whether the croissants had arrived yesterday's batch or today's.

Charles sat down and got through the first page easily enough, his name printed twice because his cursive, according to his mother, looked like a spider had fallen in the ink. The second page defeated him. It asked about allowances and dependents and something called withholding, and the small print at the top said the form was called Form W-4. He read the header three times. It said, in plain government prose, that a new employee filled this out so the employer knew how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. That much he could absorb. What he could not absorb was which boxes applied to a seventeen-year-old who had never earned a dollar in his life and whose largest prior financial decision was buying a graphing calculator with birthday money.

He texted his mother. "I'm filling out a W-4 at the coffee shop. What do I put?" Then, because staring at his phone felt useless, he photographed the form and sent that too. Across the table from him, Timothe was doing summer reading for a class neither of them had been warned would involve the word ontology, which Timothe had explained at length yesterday as basically the study of what things are, of what it means for something to exist at all. Timothe looked up from his book now and peered at the form over Charles's shoulder.

"That's a real form?" Timothe said. "It looks like something from a museum."

"It's so they know how much to take out of my paycheck," Charles said. "Tax. Federal income tax."

"Litigate it," Timothe said, which was his answer to most obstacles lately, a joke inherited from an uncle who was a lawyer and apparently said it about everything, parking tickets, bad haircuts, the price of movie popcorn. "Refuse to pay taxes on principle. Take it to the Supreme Court."

"I haven't been paid yet. There's nothing to take."

His phone buzzed. His mother had replied with a photograph of her own, a picture of a page from some tax guide she kept in the filing cabinet, with two sentences highlighted in yellow marker, and beneath it, in her terse texting style: "Just follow that. Zero dependents. You're a dependent." Charles studied the highlighted sentences, then the form, then the sentences again. The logic was not complicated once he stopped being afraid of it, and he noticed that the fear had been the actual obstacle, not the math. He filled in the boxes, chose zero, signed his name in the spider-ink cursive, and felt something settle that he could not quite name. It was not pride, exactly. It was closer to the feeling of a door that had been locked turning out to be merely heavy.

Ms. Mercado came back, collected the clipboard, and glanced over the page with the flat, unhurried competence of someone who had processed a hundred of these. "Good," she said. "Braiden never did his. Worked three weeks before I noticed." She said this without irritation, the way she seemed to say everything, phlegmatic as the old espresso machine that groaned but never quit. "You start Saturday, seven in the morning. Braiden trains you."

Braiden was a year ahead of them, and Charles had seen him behind this counter a dozen times without ever thinking of the counter as a place where paperwork lived. On Saturday he arrived at seven, and Braiden showed him the grinder, the milk fridge, the little chalkboard of prices, and the correct way to stack cups so they did not stick together. Between customers Braiden leaned on the counter and said, "So you actually did the W-4? Mom made me do mine at the kitchen table with her hovering." He shrugged. "I put down whatever she told me."

Charles wiped the steam wand with a cloth, as he had been shown, and found that he had an opinion where before there had been nothing. "I read the top of it," he said. "It tells you what it's for. I mean, it doesn't tell you what to put, that part I had to text my mom, but it tells you why it exists."

"Deep," Braiden said, but not unkindly. The door chimed and a woman came in shaking rain off her coat, though it had not been raining when Charles walked in, and Braiden was already reaching for a cup. "Medium drip, no room," he called over his shoulder, and Charles moved to the register, pressed the button he thought was right, and watched the little screen light up with a number that was, for the moment, still all his.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism described just twelve children, and The Lancet fully retracted it in 2010.
story:
The bus dropped them at the chemistry building forty minutes late, which left Maya an hour before her father's texts would stop being polite. She had until three o'clock to decide whether she would speak at the town hall on Thursday, the student slot Ms. Ross had arranged for her, and she still didn't know what she thought. Her aunt had come to the pediatrician's office with them last week for her little brother's checkup, and while they waited she had pulled up an article on her phone and held it out, saying it was why she'd waited so long to vaccinate her own kids. Maya had read enough of it in the waiting room to feel her face go hot, but she hadn't known, then, how to answer.

"Two minutes each at the station," Ms. Ross said at the door of the lab, counting heads, "and then we regroup in the seminar room, because Dr. Osei is giving us the afternoon slot only until three."

The lab smelled of ethanol and warm electronics. At the first bench a graduate student showed them a tray of pipettes and explained that she was running the same assay for the ninth time. Keagan, beside Maya, whispered that he'd die of boredom repeating one experiment forever, and the graduate student, who had heard him, said without looking up, "That's the job. One result is a rumor. Nine is a maybe."

Maya wrote that down. Below it she wrote her aunt's question, which she had been carrying around all week like a stone: how do you know the studies are true? Her aunt was not a foolish woman. She kept a ledger for a small business, could spot a padded invoice from across a room, and distrusted anything that arrived sounding too confident.

At the next station Bianca was reading a poster pinned above a freezer, a scathing review, by the look of it, of some published paper, its margins crowded with red ink. "Somebody tore these people apart," Bianca said. "Before it even got printed?"

"That's peer review," the graduate student said. "Other scientists try to break your paper before the journal prints it. And even then it's not settled until someone else repeats the work."

Maya's phone buzzed. Her father: Your aunt's coming to dinner Thursday. She wants to hear what you say. The deadline tightened in her chest. In the seminar room Dr. Osei was stacking reprints on the table, and Maya raised her hand before she lost her nerve.

"The vaccine and autism study," she said. "My aunt showed me an article about it. Was that ever real science, or was it always wrong?"

Dr. Osei pushed a reprint across the table toward her, an older one, its cover worn soft at the corners. "Look at the numbers yourself. Twelve children, that whole paper. Twelve. And it didn't hold up. The Lancet retracted it fully in 2010." She tapped the page. "Find me a consensus built on one small study and I'll show you a house on one post."

Keagan leaned over to see. "So it was in The Lancet in 1998 and nobody caught it at first?"

"Retraction is the system correcting itself," Dr. Osei said. "Slowly. Which is the honest complaint about science, that it's slow. Not that it's a lie."

Maya copied the details into her notebook, the twelve children, the 1998 paper, the full retraction in 2010, and understood, sitting there, that she had two things in her head that were both true. Her aunt's caution was not stupidity; it was a habit of checking, applied to the wrong scale. The graduate student's aphorism came back to her, one result is a rumor, and she saw that her aunt had trusted a rumor because it looked like checking. The gain and the cost arrived together: Maya could now defend the studies, but she would have to do it across a dinner table, gently, to a woman who had been trying to be careful.

At three o'clock Ms. Ross herded them toward the bus. In the corridor Maya texted her father: Tell Auntie I'll talk Thursday, and I want her to bring the article. She imagined sitting beside her aunt with the phone between them, the screen's glow on both their faces, pointing to the twelve, the year, the retraction, and then, harder, saying the thing she was less sure of, that twelve years of fear doesn't transmute into trust just because someone shows you a number.

The bus idled at the curb, doors open, exhaust ghosting in the cold. Bianca took the seat behind her and asked what she was going to say, exactly, in front of everyone.

"I'll start with what I got wrong," Maya said, and pulled the seatbelt across her lap. "That's the only opening she'll sit still for."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Nicolas spread his pencils across the long table by the library window, twelve of them in a fan, sharpened to different heights like a small skyline. He was copying a photograph of his grandmother's hands for the school show, and he had until Friday. The light through the blinds cut the paper into stripes, so he turned the drawing board a quarter turn and started again on the knuckles, pressing harder than he meant to.

A boy from his chemistry class, Abdallah, dropped into the opposite chair with a stack of books. "You're going to break the lead," Abdallah said.

"Don't call it that."

"What?"

"Lead." Nicolas held the pencil up between them, its dark core visible at the tip. "It's graphite. Pencil lead has never actually been lead, the metal. The name just comes from the 16th century, when people found graphite and thought it was a kind of lead ore."

Abdallah leaned back. "Then why does my little brother's teacher make a whole speech about not chewing pencils?"

"Because teachers are inured to saying things they've never checked." Nicolas rotated the pencil, watching the light run along the hexagon. "My cousin spent a week thinking he was poisoned because he gnawed one during a math test. I told him the same thing. He didn't believe me either."

Adriana arrived with a coffee she wasn't supposed to have in the library, holding it away from her body like evidence. She sat down, looked at the drawing, and pulled it toward her without asking. "The thumb is wrong."

"The thumb is from the photo."

"The photo is wrong, then. Grandmothers' thumbs don't bend like that. Unless yours has a war injury."

Nicolas took it back and studied it. He could see it now that she'd said it, the joint too stiff, like the hand of a mannequin. He erased it, and the graphite smeared sideways in a grey haze he would have to work back into shadow. That was the thing about pencils, he thought, the thing he liked and hated at once: everything could be undone, but undoing always left a mark.

Ms. Augustin, the librarian, passed behind them on her rounds. She paused at the smudge of eraser dust on the table, and Nicolas braced for a scolding, but she only set down a small hand broom and dustpan without a word and moved on toward the reference shelves. Abdallah watched her go. "She's the most quietly terrifying person I know. My brother calls her the polymath of the periodicals."

"She read three books while shelving one," Adriana said. "I counted."

Nicolas rebuilt the thumb from memory instead of from the photo, letting the joint soften. His grandmother's hands folded like paper, creased everywhere, and he had been drawing them stiff because the stiff version was safer, because if he drew them true, something in the drawing would ask him to say what the drawing was for. She was in a hospital forty minutes away. He had not gone to see her in two weeks. He had told his mother he had too much homework, which was a bombastic excuse coming from someone who had spent Sunday watching videos of other people drawing.

"You're doing that thing," Adriana said.

"What thing."

"Where you stop and stare at it like it insulted you."

He didn't answer. He picked up the soft 6B and laid a dark wash under the knuckles, and the stripes of window light shifted as a cloud passed, so the whole drawing went briefly flat and then came back with more depth than before. Maybe the mistake with the thumb had helped. Maybe accuracy and truth were not the same project, and a drawing could be precise about the wrong thing. He couldn't decide, and he kept drawing while he didn't decide, which felt like the only honest way to hold both ideas.

Abdallah pulled out his phone and typed something. "I'm texting my brother. No lead. He's going to owe me five dollars."

"He chewed a pencil because he thought it was already killing him," Adriana said. "That's the most fatalistic nine-year-old alive."

"He's not fatalistic, he's thorough." Abdallah hit send.

Ms. Augustin came back around, collected the dustpan, and looked at the drawing for a long moment, her finger hovering above the paper without touching it. "The thumb," she said.

"Is it wrong?"

"No. It's the only part that's alive." She tapped the table twice, almost gently, and carried the dustpan away toward the front desk, where the date stamp sat in its tray, and Nicolas sharpened his pencil and went back in.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
The library on the third floor of the humanities wing smelled like radiator dust, and Hannah had claimed the corner table by the window an hour before anyone else arrived. She spread the two articles side by side. Both asked the same question, whether students who handwrite their notes remember more than students who type, and both had found the same answer: handwriting won. One study had surveyed thirty people. The other, thirty thousand.

Mr. Sun had assigned the review two weeks ago, and it was due tomorrow at eight in the morning. He wanted a critical comparison, not a summary, and he had underlined that word twice on the assignment sheet, as though repetition could make it appear in her document. So far she had eleven hundred words of summary.

Rafaelle dropped into the chair across from her and slid a coffee across the table. "You look melancholic."

"I look like a person with eleven hundred words of summary." She turned her laptop toward him. "Both articles say the same thing. Handwriting wins. What am I supposed to compare, the fonts?"

He scrolled without reading, the way he did, then stopped. "Which one's better?"

"They're identical. That's the problem."

Amber arrived with her own stack of printouts and sat down without greeting anyone, which was her way of concentrating. She flipped one of Hannah's articles over, checked the methods section, and tapped a number. "This one's thirty people."

"The other one's thirty thousand," Hannah said. She said it as trivia, the way you'd note that one author had an idiosyncrasy in the footnotes, a habit of citing himself in the third person, which she had already decided to mention in her review because it filled half a paragraph.

Amber was still tapping. "So one of them asked thirty people and one of them asked thirty thousand, and you think they're identical?"

"They found the same thing."

"With the same certainty?"

Hannah opened her mouth and closed it. She pulled the larger study toward her and read the results section again, then the smaller one, then both, holding a sentence from each in her head at the same time. The numbers were the same. The confidence was the same on the page, the same tidy prose, the same brisk conclusion. But the smaller article's finding came from thirty people. Thirty. Her graduating class alone had been ninety.

"Say the thirty people were weird," she said slowly. "Say the typing group just happened to include five people who type fast and don't care. With thirty thousand, that washes out."

Amber shrugged. "You're the one writing the review."

Rafaelle had stopped pretending to scroll. "So what are you going to say?"

"I don't know yet." She deleted a paragraph. Then another. The word count dropped to four hundred and she felt something close to panic, and something else underneath it, closer to relief. She started typing. The larger study's finding carried more weight, she wrote, and then she stopped, because that wasn't precise enough, and precision was the entire point. She tried again. The same result from the large study meant more than the same result from the small one, because the small study's margin of error was wider. Thirty people could be skewed. Thirty thousand could not be skewed the same way.

She worked through lunch, sublimating her hunger into a kind of grim efficiency, and when Rafaelle came back with a sandwich she took half of it without looking up. He read over her shoulder in silence for a while.

"You're saying the small study is wrong," he said.

"No." She highlighted her own sentence, the one about margins, and studied it. "I'm saying the same finding isn't the same finding. The big one, I'd trust. The small one, I'd want it repeated somewhere else first." She paused. "It might still be right. I can't tell from here."

"So your conclusion is you don't know."

"My conclusion is that I know how much each one is worth, and they're not worth the same."

She wrote until the window went dark and the radiator ticked. The review ended with a comparison of the two articles' claims, weighted differently, and a final line she rewrote four times: the smaller study's result remained possible, and unconfirmed, and she left it there. She printed it at the circulation desk, and the cashier-librarian held the warm pages out to her.

"Due tomorrow?" the librarian asked.

"Eight a.m."

"Cutting it close."
